name: Accentor
hint: Sparrow-like songbird of Eurasian mountains; the dunnock is the familiar lowland species
fact: Accentors are sparrow-like birds, mostly of high mountains. The dunnock, a common garden accentor, has a complex mating system in which a female may have two mates.

name: Aerie
hint: Lofty nest of an eagle or other raptor (US spelling)
fact: Golden eagles may keep several nests in their territory and switch between them from year to year, adding fresh material each time.

name: Akepa
hint: Small Hawaiian honeycreeper; males are orange and the bill tips are slightly crossed
fact: Their slightly crossed bill tips help these birds pry open leaf buds and seed pods to reach hidden insects.

name: Alala
hint: Hawaiian name for the islands' native crow, now surviving mainly through captive breeding
fact: The alala, or Hawaiian crow, became extinct in the wild in 2002; conservationists have since worked to release captive-bred birds.

name: Albatross
hint: Huge ocean-wandering seabird with the longest wingspan of any living bird
fact: Great albatrosses have wingspans of up to about 3.5 m. A Laysan albatross named Wisdom is the oldest known wild bird, still raising chicks in her 70s.

name: Altricial
hint: Describes chicks that hatch nearly naked, blind and helpless
fact: Songbird, parrot and pigeon chicks hatch nearly naked with their eyes closed and rely entirely on their parents for food and warmth.

name: Alula
hint: Tuft of small feathers on a bird's 'thumb' that helps prevent stalling at low speed
fact: The alula is a tuft of feathers on a bird's thumb. Birds raise it during slow flight and landing, and it smooths airflow over the wing like an aircraft's slats.

name: Anhinga
hint: American 'water turkey' that swims with only its snaky neck showing
fact: It spears fish with its sharp bill and flips them to swallow head-first, then spreads its wings to dry, as its feathers aren't waterproof.

name: Antbird
hint: Tropical American perching species that follows marching insect swarms to grab fleeing prey
fact: Some species are professional army ant followers: they don't eat the ants but snap up the insects fleeing from the swarm.

name: Anting
hint: Bird habit of rubbing formic-acid-producing insects through its feathers
fact: In anting, birds rub ants on their feathers or sprawl on an ant nest, possibly because the formic acid helps control feather lice and mites.

name: Antpitta
hint: Round, long-legged, nearly tailless ground bird of Neotropical forests, most diverse in the Andes
fact: Antpittas are shy, plump, long-legged birds of Central and South American forests that are far more often heard than seen. The family has about 68 species.

name: Antshrike
hint: Neotropical insect-eater with a hooked beak; the barred species' male is striped black and white
fact: Antshrikes are antbirds named for their stout, hooked, shrike-like bills. Male barred antshrikes are boldly barred black and white, while females are rufous.

name: Apostlebird
hint: Grey Australian bush dweller that roams the ground in noisy family groups of about a dozen
fact: Apostlebirds often travel in groups of about 12, which is why they were named after the Twelve Apostles. They build mud nests and raise young cooperatively.

name: Aracari
hint: Slender, long-tailed toucan of Neotropical forests, smaller than the classic big toucans
fact: Aracaris roost together, with several birds squeezing into one tree hole and folding their tails over their backs.

name: Argus
hint: Huge Southeast Asian pheasant whose wing feathers bear rows of eyespots
fact: The great argus is named after the hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth, after the many eyespots males fan out in courtship.

name: Asity
hint: Madagascan songbird; males grow bright bare wattles around the eyes when breeding
fact: Asities live only in Madagascar; the sunbird-asities evolved long, curved bills for drinking nectar and were once called false sunbirds.

name: Auklet
hint: Small, plump seabird of the North Pacific, related to puffins; the crested kind wears a curly plume
fact: Crested auklets give off a strong citrus scent, like tangerines, which may play a part in courtship.

name: Avian
hint: Adjective meaning relating to birds
fact: Avian comes from Latin avis, bird, which also gives us aviary, aviation and even auspicious, from Roman augurs who read omens in birds.

name: Aviary
hint: Large enclosure where captive birds can fly
fact: The word comes from Latin avis, bird; ancient Romans kept large aviaries to fatten thrushes and other birds for the table.

name: Aviculture
hint: Practice of keeping and breeding birds in captivity
fact: Captive breeding saved the Guam kingfisher, which vanished from the wild in the 1980s but survived because birds had been taken into care.

name: Avifauna
hint: All the bird species of a particular region
fact: New Zealand's birds evolved with almost no land mammals; its unique species include the kiwi and the kakapo, the world's only flightless, nocturnal parrot.

name: Avocet
hint: Black-and-white wader with a long, thin, upturned bill it sweeps side to side
fact: The pied avocet is the emblem of the RSPB, chosen after the bird returned to breed in Britain in the 1940s following a century's absence.

name: Babbler
hint: Noisy Old World songbird that lives and forages in chattering family groups
fact: Jungle babblers forage in noisy gangs of six to ten, which earned them the nickname 'seven sisters' in northern India.

name: Bananaquit
hint: Small yellow-breasted nectar thief of tropical America that raids sugar bowls
fact: The bananaquit is a small nectar-feeder of the tropical Americas. Its nickname, 'sugar bird', comes from its fondness for bowls and feeders of sugar.

name: Barbet
hint: Stout, bristle-billed tropical bird related to toucans; the coppersmith is one
fact: The coppersmith barbet is named for its monotonous 'tuk-tuk-tuk' call, which sounds like a metalworker hammering copper.

name: Barbule
hint: Tiny hooked branch that zips a feather's vane together
fact: Barbules hook onto neighbouring barbs like a zip; when a bird preens, it is re-zipping any splits in its feathers.

name: Bateleur
hint: Short-tailed African eagle with a red face that rocks from side to side in flight
fact: The bateleur's name is French for 'street performer', for its tilting, acrobatic flight. It may be the origin of the Zimbabwe Bird, the national emblem of Zimbabwe.

name: Batis
hint: Small black-and-white African flycatcher, such as the chinspot
fact: The chinspot species is named for the chestnut spot on the female's chin; its descending whistle is often rendered as 'three blind mice'.

name: Baza
hint: Crested bird of prey of Africa, Asia and Australia, also called a cuckoo-hawk
fact: Bazas, genus Aviceda, have a prominent crest and two tooth-like notches on the edge of the upper bill.

name: Beak
hint: Hard, horny, toothless mouthpart every bird has
fact: A bird's beak is bone sheathed in keratin, the protein in fingernails. The sheath keeps growing throughout life as the tip wears down.

name: Bellbird
hint: Tropical American cotinga whose males have the loudest known call of any avian species
fact: The white bellbird has the loudest bird call ever recorded, up to about 125 decibels. Males may deliver it while facing a female perched nearby.

name: Besra
hint: Small Asian forest sparrowhawk, a close relative of the shikra
fact: The name besra comes from Hindi. This forest hawk flies with a distinctive 'flap-flap-glide' and builds a fresh nest every year.

name: Bevy
hint: Group of quail or larks; also any lively group
fact: Quail gather in a bevy or covey, and the 15th-century Book of St Albans, a famous list of group names, also lists a bevy of ladies.

name: Bill
hint: Another word for a bird's mouthpart, often used for a duck's flat one
fact: Ducks' bills have comb-like edges called lamellae that sieve food from water, plus a hard 'nail' at the tip for digging and grabbing.

name: Birdbath
hint: Shallow garden basin of water where sparrows splash and drink
fact: Birds bathe to clean and condition their feathers; a basin with a shallow, rough-bottomed edge lets small songbirds wade in safely.

name: Birdcage
hint: Wire enclosure for a pet canary or budgie
fact: In China, owners of songbirds traditionally carry them in ornate cages to parks in the morning so the birds can hear each other sing.

name: Birdcall
hint: Short sound a sparrow or finch makes to warn of danger or keep in touch
fact: Many small songbirds give a similar thin, high 'seet' call when a hawk flies over, and birds of other species understand it and dive for cover.

name: Birder
hint: Enthusiast who spends weekends with binoculars logging species
fact: Many birders keep a 'life list' of every species they have ever seen, and some travel the globe trying to see as many as possible.

name: Birdhouse
hint: Wooden box put up in a garden for wrens or chickadees to nest in
fact: Nest boxes for different species need different hole sizes; a small entrance keeps out bigger birds such as starlings.

name: Birding
hint: Hobby of watching feathered wildlife through binoculars
fact: The Christmas Bird Count, begun in 1900, has volunteers tally birds every winter and is one of the longest-running citizen science projects.

name: Birdseed
hint: Mix of millet, sunflower and other grains for feeders
fact: Black-oil sunflower seeds attract the widest variety of feeder birds, while cheap 'filler' grains like red millet and oats are often left uneaten.

name: Birdsong
hint: Musical sounds used to attract mates and claim territory, loudest at dawn
fact: Young songbirds learn their songs by copying adults, much as babies learn to speak, and some birds develop local 'dialects'.

name: Birdwatcher
hint: Person who observes wild feathered creatures as a hobby
fact: Roger Tory Peterson's 1934 'A Field Guide to the Birds' helped turn watching birds into a hugely popular pastime.

name: Bittern
hint: Secretive, streaky heron of reedbeds with a deep, booming call
fact: The Eurasian bittern's foghorn-like boom carries for kilometres, and when alarmed it freezes with its bill pointed skyward to blend into the reeds.

name: Blackbird
hint: European thrush whose males are jet-colored with an orange beak; a famous garden singer
fact: The common blackbird is a true thrush: only the males are black, while females are brown. It was introduced to Australia and New Zealand in the 1800s.

name: Blackcap
hint: Olive-grey Old World warbler with a rich song; the sexes differ only in the colour of their crowns
fact: Some central European blackcaps now winter in Britain instead of Spain, a new migration route that evolved within a few decades, helped by garden feeders.

name: Bluebird
hint: Small North American thrush; males are bright sky-colored, a traditional symbol of happiness
fact: The three bluebird species of the genus Sialia are thrushes that nest in tree cavities. Trails of nest boxes helped the eastern species recover from 20th-century declines.

name: Bluethroat
hint: Robin-like Eurasian songbird; males have a vivid chin patch with a red or white spot
fact: Bluethroats breed from Europe across Asia to western Alaska and winter as far away as North Africa and India. They are about the size of a European robin.

name: Bobolink
hint: Blackbird-family songbird whose breeding males look like they wear a tuxedo backwards
fact: Bobolinks breed in North American grasslands and winter in Argentina, Paraguay and Bolivia. Their old name, 'rice bird', comes from feasting on grain crops.

name: Bobwhite
hint: North American quail named after its clear, whistled call
fact: The northern bobwhite is named for its whistled 'bob-white!' call. Coveys roost on the ground in a tight circle, tails inward, to keep warm and watch for predators.

name: Boobook
hint: Small brown Australian owl named after its two-note call
fact: Its 'boo-book' call gave it its name; New Zealand's close relative is called the morepork after a similar call.

name: Booby
hint: Tropical seabird related to gannets; one species has famously bright blue feet
fact: The name may come from the Spanish 'bobo' (fool), because these tame seabirds often landed on ships and were easily caught.

name: Boubou
hint: African bush-shrike whose pairs sing perfectly timed duets
fact: Tropical boubou pairs duet so precisely, trading notes in split-second timing, that it can sound like a single bird singing.

name: Bowerbird
hint: Australasian male that builds and decorates a stage of sticks to court females
fact: Male bowerbirds build elaborate structures called bowers and decorate them with collected objects; satin bowerbirds favor anything blue, including bottle caps.

name: Brambling
hint: Orange-and-black winter finch of Europe that flocks in beech woods
fact: In winters with plentiful beech nuts, bramblings can gather in enormous roosts, with flocks in Europe reported in the millions.

name: Brant
hint: Small, dark Arctic-breeding sea goose with a white neck patch that feeds heavily on eelgrass
fact: Atlantic brant numbers crashed in the 1930s when disease wiped out the eelgrass they depend on. The North Sea's Brent oilfield is named after this goose.

name: Brent
hint: British name for a small dark sea goose that winters on estuaries
fact: These small geese breed on high-Arctic tundra and spend the winter on temperate sea coasts, where they graze heavily on eelgrass.

name: Bristlebird
hint: Shy Australian ground songster of dense coastal scrub; two of three species are endangered
fact: Bristlebirds are shy birds of Australian coastal scrub that are more often heard than seen. Two of the three species are endangered.

name: Broadbill
hint: Colorful tropical Asian songbird with a flattened beak; many hang pear-shaped nests over streams
fact: Broadbills are colorful birds of tropical Asia with wide, flattened bills. Many build pear-shaped hanging nests, often suspended over streams.

name: Brolga
hint: Tall grey Australian crane with a red band on its head, famed for its leaping dances
fact: Brolgas perform elaborate dances, bowing, leaping and trumpeting; the bird is the official bird emblem of Queensland.

name: Brood
hint: Family of young birds; or to sit on them to keep them warm
fact: Some birds raise several families a year; in a long season a pair of house sparrows may rear up to four broods.

name: Broody
hint: Describes a hen determined to sit on eggs
fact: A broody hen will sit tight for about three weeks, puffing up and growling if disturbed, and may even try to hatch dummy eggs or none at all.

name: Budgerigar
hint: Small green-and-yellow Australian parakeet, one of the world's most popular pets
fact: Wild budgerigars are green and yellow and roam Australia's dry interior in big nomadic flocks. Blue, white and other colors come from captive breeding.

name: Budgie
hint: Nickname for a small green-and-yellow Australian parakeet, a hugely popular cage bird
fact: A budgerigar named Puck set a Guinness World Record for bird vocabulary, with an estimated 1,728 words.

name: Bufflehead
hint: Tiny North American diving duck; males show a big white patch on a puffy, iridescent crown
fact: The bufflehead's name comes from 'buffalo head', for the male's oddly bulbous head. This small duck nests mostly in old tree holes dug by northern flickers.

name: Bulbul
hint: Noisy, often crested songbird of Africa and Asia; the 'nightingale' of Persian poetry
fact: In Persian and Urdu poetry the bulbul is a symbol of love, though the singer the poets had in mind was probably the nightingale.

name: Bullfinch
hint: Plump Eurasian songbird; males have a rosy-red breast and a glossy black cap
fact: Eurasian bullfinches feed heavily on tree buds in spring. Their quiet, piping 'pew' call is often described as mournful.

name: Bunting
hint: Seed-eating songbird; the indigo and painted kinds are brilliantly coloured
fact: Indigo buntings migrate at night; planetarium experiments showed young birds learn to navigate by the stars around the North Star.

name: Bushshrike
hint: Colorful African songbird family that includes gonoleks and tchagras
fact: Bushshrikes are African songbirds, many brilliantly colored. Pairs of some species, such as gonoleks, sing duets so precisely timed they sound like one bird.

name: Bushtit
hint: Tiny grey, long-tailed songbird of western North America that travels in chattering flocks
fact: Bushtits weave a long, hanging, sock-like nest from spider silk, moss and lichen, and flocks huddle together on cold nights.

name: Bustard
hint: Large, stately ground bird of grasslands and steppes; males puff up in showy courtship displays
fact: Male great bustards can weigh around 16 kg (35 lb), making them one of the heaviest animals able to fly.

name: Butcherbird
hint: Australasian songster that impales prey on thorns or wedges it in forks to eat it
fact: Butcherbirds get their name from wedging or impaling prey such as lizards and insects on branches, like meat on a hook. The pied species is a famed songster.

name: Buteo
hint: Genus of broad-winged soaring hawks, such as the red-tailed hawk
fact: In the Old World these birds are called buzzards. North Americans call them hawks and often use 'buzzard' for vultures.

name: Buttonquail
hint: Tiny partridge-like ground bird that is really a shorebird relative; females court males
fact: Buttonquails look like true quail but are related to gulls and shorebirds. Females are more colorful, court the males, and leave them to incubate the eggs.

name: Buzzard
hint: Broad-winged, soaring hawk of Europe with a mewing, cat-like call
fact: The common buzzard is now Britain's most widespread bird of prey, while in North America 'buzzard' is a folk name for vultures.

name: Cackle
hint: Loud, harsh noise a hen makes after laying
fact: Hens often make a loud racket right after laying an egg, a so-called 'egg song' whose purpose is still debated.

name: Cahow
hint: Bermuda's national bird, a petrel thought extinct for three centuries
fact: The Bermuda petrel was rediscovered in 1951 after being thought extinct since the 1600s. Careful conservation has helped it recover.

name: Canary
hint: Small yellow finch once carried into coal mines as an early-warning gas detector
fact: Canaries react to carbon monoxide before people do, so miners took them underground; British mines only phased them out in 1986.

name: Canvasback
hint: Large North American diving duck with a sloping wedge-shaped head and pale grey body
fact: The canvasback is North America's largest diving duck. Its scientific name, Aythya valisineria, comes from wild celery (Vallisneria), its favorite winter food.

name: Caracara
hint: Long-legged, crested falcon of the Americas that often walks on the ground and scavenges
fact: Caracaras are falcons that act more like vultures, walking on the ground and eating carrion. The crested caracara ranges from the southern US to Tierra del Fuego.

name: Cardinal
hint: Crested red North American songbird named after the robes of senior Catholic clergy
fact: The northern cardinal is the state bird of seven US states, more than any other bird. Unlike many songbirds, females sing too, sometimes from the nest.

name: Caruncle
hint: Fleshy, warty growth on the head of a turkey or Muscovy duck
fact: The bare head skin and caruncles of a male wild turkey can flush red, white or blue depending on how excited the bird is.

name: Casque
hint: Helmet-like growth on a hornbill's bill or a cassowary's head
fact: Most hornbill casques are light and hollow, but the helmeted hornbill's is solid, ivory-like keratin that it uses in head-butting clashes.

name: Cassowary
hint: Large flightless rainforest bird of Australia and New Guinea with a helmet-like casque
fact: Cassowaries have a dagger-like inner claw up to about 12 cm long. They are key seed dispersers, and some rainforest seeds germinate better after passing through them.

name: Catbird
hint: Grey American mimic whose mewing call sounds like a household pet
fact: The grey catbird mimics many other birds; being 'in the catbird seat' means sitting pretty in an advantageous position.

name: Cere
hint: Waxy, fleshy patch at the base of a parrot's or hawk's upper bill
fact: Named from the Latin for 'wax', the cere can reveal sex in budgerigars: adult males usually have a blue one, while females' are brown, tan or whitish.

name: Chachalaca
hint: Noisy chicken-like bird found from Texas to South America, named after its loud chorus
fact: Chachalacas are named after their raucous calls, often given by groups in a loud dawn chorus. The plain chachalaca reaches the US only in southern Texas.

name: Chaffinch
hint: Common European songbird; males have a pinkish breast and a blue-grey cap
fact: Chaffinch songs have regional dialects, and young males must hear adults to learn them properly, making the species a classic subject of birdsong research.

name: Charm
hint: Collective noun for goldfinches
fact: A group of goldfinches is a charm, from an Old English word for a noisy chatter, fitting for these twittering birds.

name: Chat
hint: Small Old World flycatcher; also a word for a casual conversation
fact: The stonechat, one of the best-known chats, is named for its call, which sounds like two pebbles being tapped together.

name: Cheep
hint: Faint, shrill peep of a young bird
fact: Chicks call loudly and urgently when cold or lost, but make soft, contented trilling sounds when warm and close to the hen.

name: Chick
hint: Fluffy baby bird, especially a newly hatched youngster of a farmyard hen
fact: Chicken chicks can walk and peck for food within hours of hatching, though the mother hen still keeps them warm under her wings.

name: Chickadee
hint: Tiny black-capped North American songbird named after its call
fact: Chickadees add extra 'dee' notes to their alarm call when a predator is more dangerous, and other small birds eavesdrop on these warnings.

name: Chicken
hint: The world's most numerous bird, domesticated from Asia's red junglefowl
fact: As of 2023 more than 26.5 billion chickens were alive, far outnumbering any other bird, and a hen bred for laying can produce over 300 eggs a year.

name: Chiffchaff
hint: Olive leaf warbler named after its simple two-note song; an early sign of European spring
fact: The common chiffchaff is named for its repetitive two-note song. It is one of the first migrant warblers to return to northern Europe each spring.

name: Chirp
hint: Short, sharp, high-pitched sound of a small bird
fact: Many small birds use brief calls to keep in touch with their flock, separate from the longer songs used to attract mates.

name: Chook
hint: Australian and New Zealand slang for a domestic chicken
fact: Chickens are the most numerous birds on Earth: in 2023 the world's chicken population was over 26 billion.

name: Chough
hint: Crow relative with a curved red or yellow bill; Cornwall's emblem bird
fact: The red-billed chough appears on Cornwall's coat of arms, and legend says the soul of King Arthur lives on in one.

name: Chukar
hint: Red-legged Asian partridge with black-barred flanks, widely introduced for hunting
fact: Chukar chicks scramble up steep slopes by flapping their wings as they run, a trick scientists study for clues to how bird flight evolved.

name: Cisticola
hint: Tiny streaky grass warbler; most of its 50-plus species live in Africa
fact: Cisticolas are tiny grassland warblers with over 50 species, most in Africa. Many look nearly identical and have descriptive names like zitting and wailing.

name: Cloaca
hint: Single rear opening birds use for eggs and waste
fact: Birds, reptiles and amphibians all have a cloaca, one all-purpose rear opening for eggs and waste. The name is Latin for 'sewer'.

name: Cluck
hint: Low, repeated sound a hen makes
fact: A mother hen uses soft calls to keep her chicks close and a rapid 'tuck-tuck-tuck' to call them over to food she has found.

name: Clutch
hint: Full set of eggs laid in one nesting attempt
fact: Clutch sizes vary hugely: albatrosses lay a single egg, while grey partridges may lay 15 or more.

name: Cockatiel
hint: Small grey Australian parrot with a yellow face, orange cheek patches and an upright crest
fact: The cockatiel is the smallest member of the cockatoo family. Native to Australia, it is one of the most popular pet birds and can learn to whistle tunes.

name: Cockatoo
hint: Crested parrot of Australasia, such as the sulphur-crested or the pink galah
fact: Cockatoos can raise and lower their showy crests. In Sydney, sulphur-crested cockatoos have learned to flip open wheelie-bin lids, a skill that spread between suburbs.

name: Cockerel
hint: Young rooster
fact: A young male chicken under a year old goes by this name; the rooster is a national symbol of France, where it is called le coq.

name: Coly
hint: Long-tailed African bird that scurries like a rodent; also called a mousebird
fact: Colies make up the bird order Coliiformes, found today only in sub-Saharan Africa. They scramble along branches and can hang upside down, looking remarkably like mice.

name: Comb
hint: Red, fleshy crest on top of a rooster's head
fact: Combs come in shapes such as single, rose, pea and walnut that help identify chicken breeds. Most are red, but Silkies have dark purple ones.

name: Condor
hint: Huge New World vulture of the Andes or California with a vast wingspan
fact: Andean condors are master gliders: a tracking study found they flap for only about 1% of their flight time, riding rising air instead.

name: Conure
hint: Small-to-medium long-tailed parrot of the Americas; the sun kind is a popular pet
fact: 'Conure' isn't a scientific group: it's an aviculture name for dozens of small, long-tailed parrots from Central and South America.

name: Convocation
hint: Collective noun for eagles
fact: Convocation means a formal assembly, and bald eagles really do convene: thousands gather each autumn on Alaska's Chilkat River to feast on salmon.

name: Coop
hint: Small shelter or pen for keeping chickens
fact: Chicken coops need perches for roosting and nest boxes for laying; to 'fly the coop' means to escape.

name: Coot
hint: Black waterbird with a white bill and forehead shield; 'bald as a' one
fact: Instead of webbed feet, coots have broad lobes on their toes, which help them swim and also walk across soft mud.

name: Corella
hint: Small white cockatoo, mostly Australian, with a short crest, pale bill and bare bluish eye-ring
fact: The long-billed corella uses its long upper bill to dig up roots, bulbs and seeds from the ground.

name: Cormorant
hint: Dark diving seabird often seen perched with its wings spread out to dry
fact: Cormorant feathers are partly wettable, which helps them dive, so they often spread their wings to dry. Fishermen in China and Japan have trained them to catch fish.

name: Corncrake
hint: Secretive rail of hay meadows whose rasping 'crex crex' call carries through the night
fact: The corncrake's scientific name, Crex crex, imitates its rasping call. It declined sharply across Europe as mechanized mowing destroyed nests in hay meadows.

name: Corvid
hint: Member of the crow family
fact: Crows, ravens, jays and magpies are among the smartest birds, and New Caledonian crows even make and use hooked tools.

name: Cotinga
hint: Tropical American bird family including umbrellabirds, bellbirds and cocks-of-the-rock
fact: The family's white bellbird has the loudest bird call ever recorded, about 125 decibels, which males blast right at nearby females.

name: Coua
hint: Large, mostly ground-dwelling cuckoo found only in Madagascar
fact: Unlike many cuckoos, couas build their own nests and raise their own young. Many have patches of bright bare skin around the eyes, like turacos.

name: Coucal
hint: Large, ground-loving cuckoo of Africa, Asia and Australia that raises its own chicks
fact: Unlike parasitic cuckoos, coucals raise their own young, with roles reversed: the smaller male does most of the parental care.

name: Courser
hint: Fast-running, long-legged plover relative of deserts and dry savannas
fact: Coursers are named for running: they chase insects across dry plains, and 'courser' is also an old word for a swift horse.

name: Courtship
hint: Displays and rituals performed to win a mate
fact: Great crested grebe pairs perform a 'weed dance', rising breast to breast on the water while each holds waterweed in its bill.

name: Covert
hint: Small feather overlapping the base of a flight feather
fact: Coverts smooth the airflow over wings and tail. A peacock's spectacular 'tail' is really a train of extremely long upper tail coverts.

name: Covey
hint: Small group of partridges, quail or grouse
fact: A covey is a small flock of game birds such as partridges or quail; bobwhite coveys roost in a tight circle facing outwards for warmth and safety.

name: Cowbird
hint: Brown-headed American songbird that lays its eggs in other species' nests
fact: Brown-headed cowbirds have been recorded laying eggs in the nests of more than 200 host species; they once followed roaming bison herds.

name: Crake
hint: Secretive short-billed rail; the corn species calls a rasping 'crex crex' at night
fact: The corn crake's scientific name, Crex crex, imitates its rasping call, which males can repeat all night long.

name: Crane
hint: Tall, long-legged bird famous for elaborate dancing displays and loud trumpeting calls
fact: In Japanese tradition, folding 1,000 origami cranes is said to grant a wish, and the red-crowned crane symbolises long life.

name: Creche
hint: Group of penguin or flamingo chicks huddling together while parents are away feeding
fact: Emperor penguin chicks gather in large groups for warmth and protection while both parents head out to sea to fetch food.

name: Crest
hint: Tuft of feathers on top of the head, like a cockatoo's
fact: Cockatoos raise and lower their head tufts to signal mood, fanning them up when excited or alarmed. Cardinals and blue jays also have crests.

name: Crop
hint: Throat pouch where many birds store food before digesting it
fact: Pigeons and doves make 'crop milk', a nutritious secretion from the crop lining that both parents feed to their newly hatched young.

name: Crossbill
hint: Red or greenish finch with an oddly shaped beak, built for prying seeds from conifer cones
fact: Crossbills' crossed mandible tips let them pry apart conifer cones to reach seeds. They breed whenever cone crops are good, even in the middle of winter.

name: Crow
hint: Clever all-black corvid; a group of them is called a murder
fact: New Caledonian crows craft hooked tools from twigs and leaves to fish grubs out of holes, one of the most impressive examples of tool-making in animals.

name: Cuckoo
hint: Bird that tricks others into raising its chicks; its call gives its name
fact: Common cuckoo eggs often mimic the host's eggs, and the newly hatched chick pushes the host's own eggs out of the nest.

name: Culmen
hint: Ridge running along the top of a bird's upper bill
fact: Ornithologists measure the culmen, the top ridge of the bill, to compare birds; the word is Latin for 'summit'.

name: Curassow
hint: Large turkey-like bird of tropical American forests, often with a curly crest
fact: Curassows are the largest members of the cracid family. Many have curled crests, and several species are threatened by hunting and forest loss.

name: Curlew
hint: Large brown wader with a very long, down-curved bill and a haunting call
fact: The Eurasian curlew is one of Europe's biggest waders, and its name is thought to imitate its rising, bubbling 'cur-lee' call.

name: Currawong
hint: Large black-and-grey Australian songbird with yellow eyes and a ringing call
fact: Currawongs are named after the call of the pied currawong. They are related to butcherbirds and the Australian magpie, and often raid other birds' nests.

name: Cutia
hint: Colourful nuthatch-like Himalayan babbler with barred flanks and a blue-grey crown
fact: Its genus name comes from 'khutya', the bird's Nepali name. It creeps along mossy branches like a nuthatch, probing for insects.

name: Cygnet
hint: Grey, fluffy young swan
fact: Cygnets often ride on a parent's back for warmth and safety; swans usually mate for life and lay clutches of three to eight eggs.

name: Dabble
hint: Feed at the water's surface or by tipping tail-up, like a mallard
fact: Dabbling ducks feed at the surface or upend, unlike diving ducks, and they can spring straight into the air to take off without a running start.

name: Dabchick
hint: Another name for the little grebe, a tiny, round diving waterbird
fact: The dabchick, or little grebe, is the smallest grebe of Europe, Asia and Africa. When disturbed it dives quickly, and it often hides among waterside plants.

name: Darter
hint: Long-necked waterbird that spears fish underwater; also called the snakebird
fact: Darters swim with only their thin neck above water, like a snake, then spread their wings to dry because their feathers get soaked.

name: Deceit
hint: Collective noun for lapwings
fact: Lapwings draw intruders away from their nests with loud calls and distraction displays, which earned them an old reputation for deceit.

name: Decoy
hint: Wooden model duck used to lure wild waterfowl
fact: Duck decoys woven from tule reeds and feathers around 2,000 years ago were found in Lovelock Cave, Nevada.

name: Dipper
hint: Chunky songbird that bobs on rocks, then walks underwater along stream beds
fact: Dippers are the only songbirds that can dive and swim underwater, where they hunt insect larvae along fast-flowing stream beds.

name: Diver
hint: British name for a loon, such as the red-throated or great northern
fact: With legs set far back on the body, these birds barely walk on land, but they can dive as deep as 60 metres chasing fish.

name: Dodo
hint: Flightless pigeon relative from Mauritius, extinct since the late 1600s
fact: The dodo was a giant flightless pigeon from Mauritius; its last widely accepted sighting was in 1662. A Dodo famously runs the Caucus-race in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

name: Dollarbird
hint: Blue-green roller of Asia and Australia with coin-like pale spots on its wings
fact: The dollarbird is a roller named for the pale, coin-shaped spots on its wings. It ranges from India, Korea and Japan to Australia.

name: Dotterel
hint: Tame plover of northern tundra and high mountains; bold white eyebrow and chestnut belly
fact: Dotterels are so tame that 'dotterel' was once used to mean an old fool. Females are brighter than males, which incubate the eggs and raise the chicks.

name: Dove
hint: Smaller member of the pigeon family; a white one symbolises peace
fact: Pigeons and doves feed their chicks 'crop milk', a nutritious secretion made in the crop by both parents. Only a few other birds, like flamingos, do anything similar.

name: Dovecote
hint: Building with rows of nesting holes for pigeons
fact: In medieval Europe dovecotes were often a privilege of the lord of the manor; pigeons were kept for meat and eggs, and their dung was prized as fertiliser.

name: Dovekie
hint: Tiny black-and-white Arctic seabird, also called the little auk
fact: Dovekies are among the most numerous seabirds in the North Atlantic, nesting in huge colonies in places like Greenland and Svalbard.

name: Dowitcher
hint: Long-billed shorebird; its two North American species are notoriously hard to tell apart
fact: Dowitchers probe mud with a rapid up-and-down 'sewing machine' motion. Their unusual name comes from Iroquois.

name: Down
hint: Soft, fluffy under-feathers used to stuff duvets
fact: These fluffy feathers lack the tiny hooks that zip other feathers flat, so they trap warm air. Eider ducks line their nests with them.

name: Drake
hint: Male duck
fact: In many ducks the male is brightly coloured while the female is mottled brown; male mallards even sport a neat curl of black tail feathers.

name: Drongo
hint: Glossy black, fork-tailed bird of Africa, Asia and Australia; Aussie slang for a fool
fact: Fork-tailed drongos in the Kalahari mimic the alarm calls of other animals to scare meerkats off their food, then swoop in and steal it.

name: Duck
hint: Waterfowl with a broad flat bill; the male is a drake
fact: Ducks keep their plumage waterproof partly by spreading oil from a preen gland at the base of the tail over their feathers while grooming.

name: Duckling
hint: Fluffy baby of a mallard or other waterbird with a flat bill
fact: Wood duck young leap from high tree-hole nests the day after hatching, often bouncing unharmed onto the ground below.

name: Dunlin
hint: Small sandpiper with a black belly patch in summer; forms huge swirling winter flocks
fact: Its name is a form of 'dunling': dun, a dull greyish-brown, plus -ling, 'one with that quality' - a good fit for its drab winter plumage.

name: Dunnock
hint: Drab brown-grey hedge bird of Europe, often mistaken for a sparrow
fact: Dunnocks have complicated love lives: a female may pair with two males at once, and both may help feed her chicks.

name: Eagle
hint: Large, powerful bird of prey with a hooked beak; a bald one is a US national symbol
fact: Bald eagle pairs reuse and add to the same nest for years, producing some of the largest tree nests ever recorded for any bird.

name: Eaglet
hint: Chick of a bald or golden bird of prey
fact: Bald eagle chicks stay in the nest for about 10 to 12 weeks, growing nearly to adult size before they take their first flight.

name: Eggshell
hint: Hard, chalky casing a chick must break out of
fact: Eggshells are mostly calcium carbonate and are dotted with thousands of tiny pores that let the developing chick breathe.

name: Egret
hint: White, heron-like wader once hunted almost to extinction for its breeding plumes
fact: Egret plumes were so prized for 19th-century hats that public outrage over the slaughter helped launch early bird-protection societies.

name: Eider
hint: Large sea duck whose soft breast down is gathered to fill luxury quilts
fact: In Iceland, farmers gather this duck's down by hand from nests, mostly after the ducklings have left; one quilt needs the down of dozens of nests.

name: Erne
hint: Old name for the white-tailed sea eagle, much loved by crossword setters
fact: The white-tailed eagle, or erne, was wiped out in Britain but reintroduced to Scotland from 1975 and, more recently, to the Isle of Wight.

name: Euphonia
hint: Small tropical American finch, often glossy blue-black above and yellow below
fact: Euphonia means 'good sound' in Greek, for these birds' pleasing calls. Many male euphonias are dark metallic blue above and bright yellow below.

name: Exaltation
hint: Collective noun for larks
fact: An exaltation of larks, recorded in the 15th century, suits skylarks, which pour out song as they rise high into the sky.

name: Eyas
hint: Young hawk taken from the nest to be trained for falconry
fact: In falconry an eyas is a hawk taken from the nest as a nestling, while a 'passager' is one trapped as a young bird on migration.

name: Eyrie
hint: Big stick nest of an eagle, high on a cliff or tree
fact: Bald eagles often reuse the same nest for years, adding sticks each season; the biggest can reach 4 m deep and weigh about a tonne.

name: Fairywren
hint: Tiny cocked-tailed Australian songbird; breeding males of the superb species are bright blue
fact: Female superb fairywrens teach a 'password' note to their chicks, which helps parents tell their own young from cuckoo chicks sneaked into the nest.

name: Falcon
hint: Swift raptor with long pointed wings; the peregrine is the most famous kind
fact: The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth, reaching over 300 km/h (about 190 mph) in its hunting dive, called a stoop.

name: Falconry
hint: Ancient art of hunting with trained birds of prey
fact: Hunting with trained hawks and falcons has been practised for thousands of years and is listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.

name: Fantail
hint: Small, restless flycatcher of Asia and Australasia; piwakawaka in Maori
fact: In Maori legend this bird caused the demigod Maui's death by laughing, waking the goddess Hine-nui-te-po as he sought immortality.

name: Feather
hint: Keratin structure found in no living animal except birds
fact: Among living animals only birds have feathers, but many dinosaurs had them too. One tundra swan was found to have more than 25,000 feathers.

name: Fernbird
hint: Streaky brown New Zealand wetland songster with a ragged, spiny-looking tail
fact: The New Zealand fernbird lives only in New Zealand, in wetlands and scrub. Its thin, spine-like tail feathers give it a ragged look.

name: Fieldfare
hint: Large grey-headed thrush that visits Britain in winter flocks, feeding on berries
fact: Fieldfares nest in loose colonies and defend them by dive-bombing predators and spraying them with droppings.

name: Figbird
hint: Fruit-eating Australasian oriole relative; males have bare red skin around the eye
fact: Figbirds are fruit-loving relatives of the orioles that often gather in noisy flocks in fruiting fig trees.

name: Finch
hint: Small seed-eating songbird with a stout cone-shaped bill; includes the canary, siskin and linnet
fact: Darwin's famous Galapagos 'finches' are actually tanagers, but their varied beaks became a classic example of evolution by natural selection.

name: Finfoot
hint: Shy, grebe-like tropical waterbird with brightly coloured, lobed toes
fact: The male sungrebe, one of the three species, carries its chicks in skin pockets under its wings, even while flying.

name: Firecrest
hint: Tiny European kinglet with a bold white eyebrow and an orange-and-yellow head stripe
fact: Along with the goldcrest, the firecrest is one of Europe's smallest birds, weighing just a few grams. Males show off their orange crest during breeding.

name: Firefinch
hint: Tiny red African seed-eater of the waxbill family
fact: Firefinches are small red African waxbills. They are the main hosts of indigobirds, which lay their eggs in firefinch nests.

name: Flamboyance
hint: Collective noun for pink wading birds famous for standing on one leg
fact: A group of flamingos is often called a flamboyance, fitting for pink birds that perform synchronised 'marching' displays in huge crowds.

name: Flamingo
hint: Pink wader that often stands on one leg and feeds with its head held upside down
fact: Flamingos get their pink color from carotenoid pigments in the algae and brine shrimp they eat. Their chicks hatch with plain grey or white down.

name: Fledge
hint: Grow flight feathers and leave the nest
fact: Young common murres leap off sea cliffs before they can fully fly, gliding down to the sea where their fathers raise them.

name: Fledgling
hint: Young bird that has recently left the nest
fact: Fledglings hopping on the ground are usually fine: their parents are often nearby, still feeding them while they learn to fly.

name: Flicker
hint: Ground-feeding woodpecker of the Americas that eats huge numbers of ants
fact: Northern flickers often feed on the ground, lapping up ants with a long, sticky, barbed tongue.

name: Flightless
hint: Unable to take to the air, like a penguin or ostrich
fact: Losing the ability to fly evolved many times, often on islands without predators; the dodo of Mauritius and the kakapo of New Zealand are famous examples.

name: Flock
hint: General word for a group of birds or sheep
fact: Birds gather for safety and to find food; flocks of red-billed queleas in Africa can contain millions of birds.

name: Flufftail
hint: Tiny, secretive rail-like bird of African marshes, far more often heard than seen
fact: Flufftails are small, secretive birds of sub-Saharan Africa and Madagascar. The white-winged species is one of Africa's rarest birds, found in Ethiopia and South Africa.

name: Flycatcher
hint: Name for many small songbirds that sally out from a perch to grab insects in midair
fact: The tyrant flycatchers of the Americas form the largest bird family on Earth, with over 400 species, including kingbirds and phoebes.

name: Flyway
hint: Major route that migrating birds follow
fact: North America has four main migration routes, the Atlantic, Mississippi, Central and Pacific, which are used to manage waterfowl.

name: Forktail
hint: Black-and-white Asian bird that hunts insects along rushing mountain streams
fact: Forktails are black-and-white Asian birds that hunt along rocky mountain streams, constantly wagging their long, deeply forked tails.

name: Fowl
hint: Chickens, turkeys, ducks and kin; 'neither fish nor ___'
fact: Fowl form a clade called Galloanserae, uniting landfowl such as chickens with waterfowl such as ducks. The domestic chicken is the most numerous bird on Earth.

name: Francolin
hint: Partridge-like game bird of Africa and southern Asia
fact: Francolins are partridge-like game birds. Many former francolins are now called spurfowl, after DNA showed they are closer to Old World quails.

name: Friarbird
hint: Large, noisy, drab honeyeater of Australasia; some have bare dark heads likened to a monk's
fact: Friarbirds, also called leatherheads, are large honeyeaters said to resemble friars. Smaller orioles mimic their plumage, using the friarbirds' aggressive reputation to avoid attacks.

name: Frigatebird
hint: Tropical ocean flier that inflates a red throat pouch in courtship and robs others of food
fact: Frigatebirds can soar for weeks on ocean winds and have the largest wing area relative to body mass of any bird. Males inflate a red throat pouch to court females.

name: Frogmouth
hint: Owl-like night bird of Asia and Australia with a huge gape; freezes to look like a broken branch
fact: Frogmouths are often mistaken for owls but are related to nightjars. The tawny frogmouth freezes with its bill pointed upward to mimic a broken branch.

name: Fulmar
hint: Gull-like tube-nosed seabird that defends its nest by spitting foul oil
fact: Its name comes from Old Norse for 'foul gull': fulmars squirt a smelly stomach oil at intruders, which can mat a predator's feathers.

name: Furcula
hint: Scientific name for a bird's fused collarbones
fact: Latin for 'little fork', the wishbone braces a bird's chest for flight. It was once thought unique to birds, but Velociraptor and other theropod dinosaurs had one too.

name: Gadwall
hint: Grey-brown dabbling duck with a black rear that often steals food from coots
fact: From afar the drake looks plain grey, but up close its plumage is an intricate pattern of fine black-and-white wavy lines.

name: Gaggle
hint: Collective noun for geese on the ground
fact: Gaggle, for geese on land or water, appears in the 15th-century Book of St Albans, and the word imitates their cackling.

name: Galah
hint: Pink-and-grey Australian cockatoo; also slang for a silly person
fact: Galahs are among Australia's most abundant and widespread birds. In Aussie slang a 'galah' is a loud, foolish person, likely inspired by their noisy, clownish flocks.

name: Gallinule
hint: Moorhen relative; the purple species walks across lily pads on very long toes
fact: The purple gallinule's long toes spread its weight so it can walk across lily pads. It sports purple-blue plumage, a red-and-yellow bill and a pale blue forehead shield.

name: Gander
hint: Male goose
fact: Male geese are fiercely protective, standing guard while their mate incubates the eggs; most geese pair for life.

name: Gannet
hint: Large white seabird that plunge-dives for fish; British slang for a greedy eater
fact: Gannets hit the sea at up to about 100 km/h (60 mph); air sacs in their face and chest help cushion the impact of each dive.

name: Gape
hint: Wide, often brightly coloured mouth of a begging chick
fact: Many nestlings have bright yellow, orange or red mouth linings that stand out in a dark nest and trigger parents to stuff food in.

name: Garganey
hint: Small dabbling duck; males have a bold white stripe curving back over the eye
fact: The garganey is strictly migratory: the entire population leaves its breeding grounds to winter in Africa, South Asia and Australasia.

name: Gizzard
hint: Muscular stomach that grinds food, often with swallowed grit
fact: Having no teeth, many birds swallow small stones that sit in this muscular stomach and grind up seeds and other tough food.

name: Glede
hint: Old British country name for the red kite
fact: The red kite nearly vanished from Britain and survived only in Wales. Reintroductions since 1989 have made it common again in England and Scotland.

name: Glide
hint: Fly without flapping, gradually losing height
fact: Albatrosses can travel for hours without flapping, using a technique called dynamic soaring to harvest energy from the wind over the waves.

name: Gnatcatcher
hint: Tiny, slim blue-grey American songbird that flicks its long tail while hunting insects
fact: Gnatcatchers build tiny cup nests bound with spider silk and covered in lichen. The blue-gray species is the most widespread in North America.

name: Gnateater
hint: Small, round, long-legged South American forest bird, often with a white tuft behind the eye
fact: Gnateaters are a small family of plump, long-legged, short-tailed birds of South and Central America. Many males have a white tuft behind the eye.

name: Goatsucker
hint: Old name for a nightjar, from a myth that it stole milk from farm animals
fact: Nightjars were called goatsuckers from an ancient myth that they drank goats' milk at night. Their family name, Caprimulgidae, means 'goat-milker' in Latin.

name: Gobble
hint: Loud, rattling call of a male turkey
fact: Male wild turkeys call to attract hens in spring and often 'shock gobble' in reply to sudden loud noises such as thunder or an owl's hoot.

name: Godwit
hint: Long-billed wader; the bar-tailed kind holds the record for the longest nonstop bird flight
fact: In 2022 a five-month-old bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,500 km (8,400 mi) nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania in 11 days, a record for a bird.

name: Goldcrest
hint: Tiny olive kinglet, among Europe's smallest birds, with a yellow-and-black stripe on its head
fact: Weighing only about 5 to 6 grams, goldcrests are among Europe's smallest birds, yet many cross the North Sea each autumn.

name: Goldeneye
hint: Black-and-white diving duck; drakes have a puffy dark green head with a round white patch by the bill
fact: Goldeneyes nest in tree cavities, and their wings make a distinctive whistling sound in flight, earning them the nickname 'whistler'.

name: Goldfinch
hint: Bright yellow-and-black seed-eater that loves thistles; state bird of Iowa, New Jersey and Washington
fact: American goldfinches nest late in summer, when thistles have gone to seed, and line their nests with thistle down. They eat an almost entirely vegetarian diet.

name: Goosander
hint: British name for the largest sawbill duck; males are white with a dark green head
fact: The goosander, called common merganser in North America, nests in tree holes. Its ducklings leap to the ground soon after hatching and follow their mother to water.

name: Goose
hint: Large honking waterfowl that migrates in V-formation; the male is a gander
fact: Flying in a V-formation lets these birds save energy by riding the upwash from the bird ahead, and they take turns in the lead.

name: Goshawk
hint: Large, fierce forest raptor prized by falconers; adults are grey with red eyes
fact: Its name comes from Old English for 'goose hawk', and the Azores islands take their name from acor, the Portuguese word for this bird.

name: Gosling
hint: Young goose
fact: Canada goose families sometimes merge into 'creches', with a few adults guarding dozens of youngsters from several broods.

name: Grackle
hint: Glossy, iridescent blackbird with a long keel-shaped tail and staring yellow eyes
fact: Grackles are known for 'anting', rubbing ants over their feathers, possibly so the ants' acid helps control parasites.

name: Grasswren
hint: Streaky, cocked-tail Australian songbird of spinifex and rocky outback
fact: Grasswrens are secretive, streaky relatives of the fairywrens that live in spinifex grass and rocky country, mostly in inland Australia.

name: Grebe
hint: Diving waterbird with lobed toes; great crested pairs perform a courtship 'weed dance'
fact: These birds eat their own feathers, possibly to form pellets that protect their stomachs from sharp fish bones.

name: Greenfinch
hint: Olive-colored European songbird with bright yellow wing flashes; a garden feeder regular
fact: European greenfinch numbers in Britain fell sharply after 2006 because of trichomonosis, a parasitic disease spread at garden bird feeders.

name: Greenshank
hint: Grey-and-white Eurasian wader with long olive legs and a slightly upturned bill
fact: The common greenshank breeds in northern bogs from Scotland to Siberia, then migrates to winter as far away as southern Africa and Australia.

name: Greyhen
hint: Female black grouse
fact: Female black grouse are mottled brown, while males are glossy black with lyre-shaped tails and gather at dawn leks to display.

name: Grosbeak
hint: Name for several stout finches and cardinals with massive, seed-cracking bills
fact: The name comes from French 'grosbec', meaning 'large beak'. Grosbeaks are not one natural group: some are finches, others are cardinals, and one is a weaver.

name: Grouse
hint: Plump game bird of moors and forests with feathered legs; the ptarmigan is one
fact: In spring, male sage-grouse gather on display grounds called leks, puffing out yellow air sacs that make loud popping sounds.

name: Guan
hint: Turkey-like, tree-dwelling bird of Central and South American forests
fact: Guans share the family Cracidae with curassows and chachalacas. The peculiar horned guan of Mexico and Guatemala wears a red horn, though it isn't a true guan.

name: Guano
hint: Built-up seabird droppings, once prized as fertilizer
fact: Seabird guano was so valuable in the 1800s that the USA passed the Guano Islands Act to claim islands, and Spain and Peru fought over the Chincha Islands.

name: Guillemot
hint: Black-and-white auk of northern seas that lays its egg on bare cliff ledges
fact: Common guillemot eggs vary so much in color and pattern that parents can recognize their own on crowded cliff ledges. North Americans call the bird a murre.

name: Gull
hint: Noisy, adaptable seabird of beaches and harbours, infamous for snatching chips
fact: Gulls are resourceful feeders: many carry shellfish into the air and drop them onto rocks or roads to crack them open.

name: Gyrfalcon
hint: Largest of its kind: an Arctic raptor in white, grey or dark forms, prized by medieval kings
fact: The gyrfalcon is the largest falcon species. In medieval falconry it was so prized that it was reserved for kings.

name: Hackle
hint: Long, narrow neck feather of a rooster, prized by fly-tiers
fact: Rooster neck feathers are prized for tying fishing flies, and the phrase 'raise one's hackles' comes from birds and dogs bristling when angry.

name: Hallux
hint: A bird's first toe, usually the one that points backwards
fact: In perching birds the hallux points backwards, opposing the three front toes, so the foot can wrap securely around a branch.

name: Hamerkop
hint: Brown African wader whose crest and bill give its head a mallet-like shape
fact: The hamerkop builds a huge domed nest of sticks and mud, often over a meter across, that other animals may later move into. Its name is Afrikaans for 'hammerhead'.

name: Harrier
hint: Slim, low-gliding marsh raptor with an owl-like face
fact: Harriers have owl-like facial discs that funnel sound to their ears, so they can hunt partly by hearing as they glide low over grassland.

name: Hatch
hint: Break out of an egg, as a chick does
fact: Quail chicks make clicking sounds inside their eggs, which helps the whole clutch break out within a few hours of each other.

name: Hatchling
hint: Baby bird that has just broken out of its egg
fact: Many newborn birds use a tiny 'egg tooth' on the tip of the beak to crack the shell; it falls off or is reabsorbed soon afterwards.

name: Hawfinch
hint: Big-headed Eurasian seed-eater with a huge bill strong enough to crack cherry stones
fact: The hawfinch's massive bill can crack cherry stones to reach the kernel inside. It is the only living species in its genus, Coccothraustes.

name: Hawk
hint: Sharp-eyed raptor; the red-tailed and Cooper's are familiar North American ones
fact: The red-tailed hawk's piercing scream is so dramatic that TV and films often use it as a generic raptor sound, even when the bird on screen is a different species.

name: Heron
hint: Long-legged wading bird that stands motionless in shallows before spearing fish
fact: Herons fly with their necks folded back in an S-shape, unlike storks and cranes, which fly with their necks stretched out.

name: Heronry
hint: Treetop colony where tall grey wading birds nest together
fact: Grey herons often return to the same treetop colonies year after year; Britain has counted its heronries' nests annually since 1928.

name: Hide
hint: Camouflaged shelter from which birdwatchers watch birds
fact: Reserves build these shelters beside lakes and marshes so people can see birds up close without disturbing them; Americans call them blinds.

name: Hihi
hint: Rare New Zealand honeyeater-like bird, also known as the stitchbird
fact: The hihi is so distinctive it has its own family, Notiomystidae. Once wiped out everywhere but Little Barrier Island, it has been reintroduced to several sanctuaries.

name: Hoatzin
hint: South American 'stinkbird' whose chicks have claws on their wings
fact: It ferments leaves in its crop like a cow, giving it a manure-like smell; chicks use wing claws to climb back up after dropping into water.

name: Hobby
hint: Small, dashing falcon that catches dragonflies and swallows in flight
fact: Eurasian hobbies often eat dragonflies on the wing, passing them from talons to beak in mid-flight.

name: Hoiho
hint: Maori name for the yellow-eyed penguin, one of the rarest penguins
fact: These penguins live only in New Zealand and appear on its $5 banknote. Unlike most penguins, they nest out of sight of one another.

name: Honeyeater
hint: Large Australasian family of nectar-sippers with brush-tipped tongues
fact: Honeyeaters are one of the largest bird families in Australasia, with about 195 species, roughly half native to Australia. Many are key pollinators of native plants.

name: Honeyguide
hint: African bird that leads people to wild bees' nests to feast on the leftover wax
fact: Greater honeyguides lead people to bees' nests and then eat the leftover wax. In Mozambique they respond to a special call used by Yao honey-hunters.

name: Honk
hint: Loud, nasal call of a goose, also the sound of a car horn
fact: Canada geese often honk in flight, which is thought to help flock members keep in touch as they travel in V formation.

name: Hoopoe
hint: Pinkish-buff bird with a fan-like, black-tipped crest and zebra-striped wings
fact: The hoopoe is named after its soft 'oop-oop-oop' call, and in 2008 it was voted the national bird of Israel.

name: Hoot
hint: Deep, hollow call of an owl
fact: The famous 'twit-twoo' of the tawny owl is usually a duet: the female calls 'ke-wick' and the male answers with a hoot.

name: Hornbill
hint: Tropical Old World bird with a huge down-curved beak often topped by a casque
fact: Most female hornbills seal themselves inside a tree-hole nest with mud and droppings, leaving a narrow slit through which the male passes food.

name: Hornero
hint: South American ovenbird that builds a dome-shaped mud nest
fact: The rufous hornero, Argentina's national bird, builds a mud nest shaped like an old wood-fired oven; its name comes from Spanish horno, 'oven'.

name: Hover
hint: Stay in one spot in mid-air, like a hummingbird or kestrel
fact: Hummingbirds stay still in mid-air by sweeping their wings in a figure-eight; the kestrel does it by facing into the wind, hence its old name 'windhover'.

name: Huia
hint: Extinct NZ wattlebird; males and females had strikingly different bills
fact: Huia tail feathers, glossy black with white tips, were treasured by Maori and worn by people of high rank. The last confirmed sighting was in 1907.

name: Hummingbird
hint: Tiny nectar-feeder of the Americas that can hover and even fly backwards
fact: The bee hummingbird of Cuba, about 5 to 6 cm long, is the smallest living bird. Hummingbirds can hover in place and even fly backwards.

name: Hylia
hint: Small olive African forest songbird; the green species skulks in undergrowth
fact: The green hylia puzzled scientists for decades: long placed near the Cettia bush warblers, in 2019 it was moved to a new family of its own, the Hyliidae.

name: Ibis
hint: Long-legged wader with a down-curved bill, sacred in ancient Egypt
fact: The sacred ibis was linked to Thoth, the Egyptian god of wisdom and writing, and huge numbers of ibises were mummified as offerings.

name: Ibisbill
hint: Grey Himalayan wader of shingle rivers with a crimson, down-curved beak and black face
fact: The ibisbill is so distinctive that it is placed in its own family. It lives on stony riverbeds in the high mountains of Central Asia and the Himalayas.

name: Imprinting
hint: Early learning that makes goslings follow the first thing they see
fact: Konrad Lorenz famously showed that newly hatched greylag geese would bond with him and follow him around as if he were their mother.

name: Incubate
hint: Keep eggs warm until they hatch
fact: Male emperor penguins incubate a single egg on their feet for about two months of the Antarctic winter, eating nothing the whole time.

name: Incubation
hint: Period when a parent keeps eggs warm until they hatch
fact: Megapodes such as the malleefowl don't sit on their eggs; they bury them in mounds of rotting vegetation or warm sand to keep them warm.

name: Indigobird
hint: Small African finch that lays its eggs in other finches' nests and copies their songs
fact: Indigobirds are brood parasites that lay their eggs mostly in firefinch nests. Males learn and mimic the songs of their host species.

name: Iora
hint: Small yellow-and-green songbird of South and Southeast Asia
fact: The iora family has just four species, all in the genus Aegithina. They were once grouped with the leafbirds and fairy-bluebirds.

name: Jabiru
hint: Huge American stork with a black head and a red band at the base of its neck
fact: The jabiru is the tallest flying bird in Central and South America; its name comes from Tupi-Guarani and means 'swollen neck'.

name: Jacamar
hint: Slim, iridescent tropical American bird with a long needle bill that catches butterflies
fact: Jacamars snatch butterflies and dragonflies in flight, then beat them against a branch to knock off the wings before eating.

name: Jacana
hint: Tropical wader with enormously long toes that let it walk on lily pads
fact: In many jacanas roles are reversed: females defend territories holding several males, and the males incubate the eggs and raise the chicks.

name: Jackdaw
hint: Small grey-naped crow with pale eyes that often nests in chimneys
fact: Jackdaws pair for life, and experiments show they can follow human gaze, reacting to where a person is looking.

name: Jaeger
hint: North American name for the three smaller skuas, piratical seabirds of the Arctic
fact: The name is German for 'hunter'. These seabird pirates chase terns and gulls in flight until they drop or cough up their catch, then grab it.

name: Junco
hint: Grey North American sparrow with white outer tail feathers, nicknamed the snowbird
fact: Its name seems to come from the Spanish word for rushes, yet juncos are seldom found among rush plants and prefer dry ground.

name: Junglefowl
hint: Wild Asian pheasant-family bird; the red species is the ancestor of the domestic chicken
fact: The red junglefowl of South and Southeast Asia is the main wild ancestor of the domestic chicken, now the most numerous bird on Earth.

name: Kagu
hint: Crested, pale grey, nearly flightless bird found only in New Caledonia
fact: The kagu has 'nasal corns' covering its nostrils, a feature found in no other bird. It is a treasured emblem of New Caledonia, and pairs duet in the mornings.

name: Kaka
hint: Large olive-brown New Zealand forest parrot, a close cousin of the kea
fact: After being reintroduced at Wellington's Zealandia sanctuary, New Zealand kākā have spread across the city and now visit suburban gardens.

name: Kakapo
hint: Flightless, nocturnal, moss-green New Zealand parrot; the world's heaviest parrot
fact: The kakapo is the world's only flightless parrot; males 'boom' deep calls from bowl-shaped hollows to attract females.

name: Kaki
hint: Critically rare New Zealand wader with black plumage and long pink legs
fact: The kakī, or black stilt, is one of the world's rarest wading birds. Most of the wild population breeds in the Mackenzie Basin of the South Island.

name: Kalij
hint: Crested Himalayan pheasant, introduced to Hawaii's Big Island
fact: Old books spelled its name 'kaleege'. Males are glossy blue-black and females brown, and both sexes have a bare red face.

name: Keel
hint: Blade-like ridge on the breastbone that anchors flight muscles
fact: The keel gives the big flight muscles room to attach. Flightless ostriches and emus lack one and have a flat, raft-shaped breastbone instead.

name: Kereru
hint: Large, iridescent green-and-white New Zealand wood pigeon
fact: The kereru is a vital seed disperser: it's one of the few surviving New Zealand birds able to swallow the large fruits of some native trees.

name: Kestrel
hint: Small falcon famous for hovering motionless over roadside verges
fact: Its name comes via French from crecelle, a ratchet, and it hunts by hovering 10-20 m above open country before swooping onto voles, lizards or insects.

name: Kettle
hint: Group of hawks circling on a thermal, like water on the boil
fact: Migrating broad-winged hawks gather in swirling groups of thousands, spiralling up on thermals before gliding south.

name: Killdeer
hint: American plover named after its shrill call; fakes a broken wing to lure predators
fact: Killdeer often nest on open gravel, even in parking lots and on flat gravel roofs, where their speckled eggs blend in with the stones.

name: Kingbird
hint: Bold American tyrant flycatcher known for attacking hawks and crows that come near
fact: Kingbirds fiercely defend their nests, chasing and even landing on the backs of crows and hawks. The eastern species' scientific name is Tyrannus tyrannus.

name: Kingfisher
hint: Colorful dagger-billed bird that dives headfirst from a perch to snatch prey from water
fact: The streamlined beak of the common kingfisher inspired engineers redesigning the nose of Japan's Shinkansen bullet train to cut noise when exiting tunnels.

name: Kinglet
hint: Tiny olive songbird with a bright crown stripe, among the smallest songbirds
fact: Weighing only about 6 grams, golden-crowned kinglets survive frigid winter nights by huddling together for warmth.

name: Kite
hint: Graceful bird of prey that shares its name with a toy flown on a string
fact: Red kites were almost wiped out in Britain, but reintroductions that began in 1989 were a huge success, and the fork-tailed raptors are now a common sight again.

name: Kittiwake
hint: Small cliff-nesting gull named after its call; the common species has black legs
fact: Kittiwakes spend most of the year far out at sea. In Newcastle, England, a famous colony nests on the Tyne Bridge and riverside buildings instead of sea cliffs.

name: Kiwi
hint: Flightless, nocturnal New Zealand bird with nostrils at the tip of its long bill
fact: Kiwi lay enormous eggs for their size, up to about a fifth of the female's body weight. They are the smallest living ratites, the group that includes ostriches and emus.

name: Knot
hint: Chunky Arctic-breeding sandpiper, red in summer; shares its name with a tied rope
fact: Red knots are champion migrants. Each spring huge numbers stop at Delaware Bay, USA, to refuel on horseshoe crab eggs on their way to the Arctic.

name: Koel
hint: Large fruit-eating cuckoo of Asia and Australia; males are glossy black with red eyes
fact: Koels are brood parasites. In India the Asian koel often lays its eggs in crows' nests, leaving the crows to raise its chicks.

name: Kokako
hint: Blue-grey New Zealand wattlebird famed for its haunting, organ-like song
fact: The North Island kokako has bright blue wattles and appears on New Zealand's $50 banknote; it prefers bounding through trees to flying.

name: Kookaburra
hint: Big Australian tree kingfisher famous for its loud laughing call
fact: The laughing kookaburra's raucous call is often used in films as a jungle sound effect. Although they are kingfishers, kookaburras rarely fish, eating insects, lizards and snakes.

name: Lammergeier
hint: Bone-eating Old World vulture that drops bones onto rocks to smash them
fact: The lammergeier, or bearded vulture, eats a diet that is 70-90% bone, dropping large bones from a height to crack them. It stains its feathers orange by bathing in iron-rich mud.

name: Lanner
hint: Large falcon of Africa, southeast Europe and the Middle East that hunts birds and bats
fact: The lanner may have been ancient Egypt's sacred falcon: gods such as Ra and Horus were often shown as a man with a lanner falcon's head.

name: Lapwing
hint: Crested black-and-white plover with a 'peewit' call and tumbling display flights
fact: The northern lapwing was once so common in Britain that its eggs were sold as a delicacy, until the law stepped in to protect them.

name: Lark
hint: Ground-nesting songbird famous for singing as it rises high over fields
fact: The skylark sings non-stop while climbing high into the sky, inspiring Shelley's poem 'To a Skylark' and Vaughan Williams's 'The Lark Ascending'.

name: Leafbird
hint: Bright green songbird of South and Southeast Asian forests; some species are skilled mimics
fact: Leafbirds are bright green songbirds of South and Southeast Asia that eat nectar, fruit and insects. Some are skilled mimics of other birds.

name: Lekking
hint: Males gathering at a display ground to show off to females
fact: Male sage-grouse gather on traditional display grounds each spring, strutting and inflating bare air sacs on their chests while females choose.

name: Leucism
hint: Partial loss of pigment that gives birds white or pale patches
fact: Unlike albino birds, leucistic birds keep their normal eye colour, because the condition reduces pigment in feathers and skin but not in the eyes.

name: Lifer
hint: Birder's term for a species seen for the first time
fact: Birders celebrate a new species by adding it to their life list, and some will cross continents to chase a single one.

name: Limpkin
hint: Brown, crane-like wading bird that specialises in eating apple snails
fact: It probably owes its name to its seemingly limping walk, and its eerie wailing cries earned it the nickname 'crying bird'.

name: Linnet
hint: Small brown finch; breeding males have a crimson forehead and breast
fact: The linnet is named for its love of flax seeds (linseed), and its scientific name Linaria also derives from linum, Latin for flax.

name: Longclaw
hint: Ground-dwelling African grassland bird of the pipit family, often with a bright throat and black necklace
fact: Longclaws are African grassland birds named for their very long hind claws. The yellow-throated longclaw looks strikingly like the unrelated American meadowlarks.

name: Longspur
hint: Sparrow-like bird of Arctic tundra and North American prairies; a close relative of the snow bunting
fact: Longspurs are named for the long claw on their hind toe. The Lapland longspur breeds across the Arctic tundra of both North America and Eurasia.

name: Loon
hint: North American name for a diver, famed for its haunting, yodelling call
fact: The common loon appears on Canada's one-dollar coin, which is why Canadians nicknamed the coin the 'loonie'.

name: Lore
hint: Area between a bird's eye and the base of its bill
fact: In some herons and egrets this small patch of bare skin changes colour in breeding season; a great egret's turns bright lime green.

name: Lorikeet
hint: Brilliantly colored Australasian parrot with a brush-tipped tongue for nectar
fact: Lorikeets have brush-like tips on their tongues for lapping up nectar and pollen. Rainbow lorikeets are a common, noisy sight in Australian cities.

name: Lory
hint: Brightly coloured, nectar-feeding parrot with a brush-tipped tongue
fact: Lories and lorikeets use brush-tipped tongues to lap up nectar and pollen, and they are among the most vividly coloured of all parrots.

name: Lovebird
hint: Small African parrot kept as a pet, named for pairs that sit close together
fact: Lovebirds are small parrots of the African genus Agapornis. Rosy-faced lovebird females carry nesting strips tucked among their rump feathers.

name: Lyrebird
hint: Australian ground-dweller famed for mimicking chainsaws, camera shutters and other species
fact: Lyrebirds are superb mimics that copy other birds and even human-made sounds. The superb species appears on the back of Australia's 10-cent coin.

name: Macaw
hint: Large, long-tailed, brightly coloured parrot of Central and South America
fact: The hyacinth macaw is the longest flying parrot species; its powerful beak can crack hard palm nuts.

name: Magpie
hint: Long-tailed black-and-white crow relative, wrongly said to steal shiny things
fact: The Eurasian magpie is one of the few non-mammals shown to recognise itself in a mirror, a sign of self-awareness.

name: Maleo
hint: Sulawesi megapode that buries its huge eggs in sun-warmed sand or volcanic soil
fact: Maleo eggs are about five times the size of a chicken's; chicks dig themselves out and can fly on the day they emerge.

name: Malkoha
hint: Large, long-tailed Asian cuckoo with a colourful bill and eye patch
fact: The name comes from Sinhala mal-koha, 'flower cuckoo', the local name for Sri Lanka's red-faced species.

name: Mallard
hint: Common dabbling duck; the drake has a glossy green head and white neck ring
fact: Almost all domestic duck breeds descend from the mallard, and only the female makes the classic loud 'quack'.

name: Malleefowl
hint: Australian ground bird that incubates its eggs in a huge compost mound it tends
fact: Male malleefowl build huge mounds of sand and rotting leaves, adding or removing sand to keep the eggs at a steady temperature. Chicks get no parental care.

name: Mamo
hint: Extinct black-and-yellow Hawaiian honeycreeper with a long curved bill
fact: The Hawaii mamo's golden feathers were prized for royal Hawaiian featherwork, including the famous yellow cloak of Kamehameha I.

name: Manakin
hint: Small, stubby tropical songbird whose males perform snappy courtship dances
fact: The male club-winged manakin 'sings' with its wings, rubbing specialised feathers together to make a violin-like tone.

name: Mandible
hint: Upper or lower half of a bird's bill
fact: Crossbills have crossed tips to their upper and lower mandibles, which lets them lever open conifer cones to extract the seeds.

name: Manucode
hint: Glossy black-purple bird-of-paradise of New Guinea whose sexes look alike
fact: Manucodes are glossy birds-of-paradise from New Guinea. Unlike most of their family, they are monogamous and males and females look alike.

name: Marabou
hint: Huge, bald-headed African stork that scavenges alongside vultures
fact: The marabou stork has one of the largest wingspans of any land bird, reportedly up to about 3.2 m (10.5 ft).

name: Martin
hint: Swallow relative; the purple kind nests in gourds and multi-room houses people put up
fact: In eastern North America purple martins nest almost only in human-provided housing, a tradition that began with Native Americans hanging gourds.

name: Mavis
hint: Old poetic and Scottish name for the song thrush
fact: The song thrush repeats each phrase two or three times, and it smashes snail shells on a favourite stone called an anvil.

name: Meadowlark
hint: Open-country songbird with a yellow breast and black V; the western species is state bird of six states
fact: Western and eastern meadowlarks look nearly identical and are best told apart by song. Despite the name, they are not larks but members of the blackbird family.

name: Megapode
hint: Big-footed Australasian ground bird that buries its eggs in mounds or warm soil
fact: Megapodes don't sit on their eggs; they bury them in mounds or warm soil. Chicks hatch fully feathered and able to run, and some can fly on their first day.

name: Merganser
hint: Fish-eating diving duck with a thin, serrated beak, nicknamed 'sawbill'
fact: Mergansers have saw-like serrations along their narrow bills for gripping slippery fish. Unlike most ducks, they feed mainly on fish.

name: Merle
hint: Archaic or Scots word for the common blackbird
fact: From the Latin merula; the male common blackbird is black with an orange-yellow bill and a rich, melodious song, while the female is brown.

name: Merlin
hint: Small, dashing falcon of northern moors and forests that hunts small birds in fast, low flight
fact: It shares its name with King Arthur's wizard. In medieval falconry the merlin was a lady's falcon, famed for chasing skylarks in spiralling flights.

name: Mesia
hint: Colourful Asian babbler with silver ear patches, related to the red-billed leiothrix
fact: The silver-eared mesia is a vividly coloured babbler of Himalayan and Southeast Asian forests, often kept as a cage bird.

name: Mesite
hint: Small, rarely flying, ground-dwelling bird found only on Madagascar
fact: Mesites form an ancient bird family of just three species, all living on Madagascar; though they have wings, they seldom fly.

name: Migrate
hint: Travel seasonally between breeding and wintering areas
fact: Arctic terns fly from their Arctic breeding grounds to the Antarctic and back every year, the longest migration of any bird.

name: Migration
hint: Seasonal long-distance journey made by many birds
fact: In 2022 a young bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,500 km nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania, a record for nonstop bird flight.

name: Miner
hint: Aggressive Australian honeyeater; noisy and bell species live in loud colonies
fact: Noisy miners are native but so aggressive that they drive smaller birds out of their territories, reducing woodland bird diversity.

name: Minivet
hint: Slim Asian songbird; in many species males are flame-red and black, females yellow and grey
fact: Minivets often travel through the forest canopy in noisy flocks, the bright males and females flashing red and yellow among the leaves.

name: Minla
hint: Small Himalayan babbler; the red-tailed species has bold black-and-white head stripes
fact: The red-tailed minla is the only species in its genus; it often joins mixed-species feeding flocks in mountain forests from the Himalayas to Vietnam.

name: Mobbing
hint: Small birds ganging up to harass an owl or hawk
fact: Songbirds often gang up on a roosting owl, calling loudly and diving at it; birders can find hidden owls by following the commotion.

name: Mockingbird
hint: Grey North American songster that imitates other species, car alarms and more
fact: A male northern mockingbird may learn around 200 songs in its life. It is the state bird of five US states, including Texas and Florida.

name: Mohua
hint: Maori name for the yellowhead, a canary-coloured South Island songbird
fact: This bird appears on New Zealand's $100 banknote. Rats and stoats threaten it in its beech forest home.

name: Mollymawk
hint: Sailors' name for the medium-sized albatrosses of the Southern Hemisphere
fact: Mollymawks are the most common albatrosses of the Southern Hemisphere. Their name comes from Dutch 'mallemok', meaning 'foolish gull'.

name: Molt
