hint: Shed old feathers and grow new ones (US spelling)
fact: Penguins undergo a 'catastrophic molt', losing all their feathers at once and fasting on land for weeks until the new ones grow in.

name: Monal
hint: Iridescent Himalayan pheasant; the Himalayan species is Nepal's national bird
fact: In Nepal it is called the danphe. Males shimmer in metallic green, purple and copper, and the scientific name honours Lady Mary Impey, wife of a judge in Bengal.

name: Moorhen
hint: Dark pond rail with a red forehead shield and a yellow-tipped bill
fact: The 'moor' in its name doesn't mean moorland; it's an old word for marsh, where these birds live.

name: Morepork
hint: Small brown owl of New Zealand named for its two-note call; Maori name ruru
fact: The morepork, or ruru, is New Zealand's only surviving native owl. Its name imitates its distinctive two-note call.

name: Motmot
hint: Tropical American bird with a racket-tipped tail it swings like a pendulum
fact: Motmots wag their racket-tipped tails when they spot a predator, apparently signalling 'I see you' so the hunter gives up.

name: Moult
hint: Shed and replace old feathers
fact: Most birds moult at least once a year, and many ducks shed all their flight feathers at once, leaving them flightless for several weeks.

name: Mousebird
hint: Long-tailed African perching species that scurries through bushes like a rodent
fact: Mousebirds are named for how they scurry through foliage. Their order, Coliiformes, is now confined to sub-Saharan Africa, but fossils show it once lived in Europe and North America.

name: Munia
hint: Small seed-eating Asian finch, such as the scaly-breasted or the white-rumped
fact: The scaly-breasted munia is sold as the nutmeg mannikin or spice finch; it lives in sociable flocks and has been introduced to places such as Hawaii and Puerto Rico.

name: Murder
hint: Collective noun for crows
fact: Calling a group of crows a murder dates back to at least the 15th century, probably inspired by old folklore linking crows with death.

name: Murmuration
hint: Collective noun for starlings, famed for swirling dusk displays
fact: In a murmuration, thousands of starlings twist in unison as each bird tracks its six or seven nearest neighbours, confusing hunting falcons.

name: Murre
hint: Black-and-white auk that lays one pointed egg on bare cliff ledges; also called a guillemot
fact: Murre eggs vary so much in colour and pattern that parents can recognise their own on crowded ledges. Underwater they 'fly' with their wings, diving as deep as 180 m.

name: Murrelet
hint: Small North Pacific auk; the marbled species nests high in old-growth trees
fact: The marbled murrelet is a seabird that nests on mossy branches of old-growth trees, often far inland. Its nest was not found by scientists until 1974.

name: Muster
hint: Old collective noun for peacocks, also a gathering of troops
fact: A muster of peacocks appears in the 15th-century Book of St Albans; the word also means an assembly of soldiers for inspection.

name: Myna
hint: South Asian starling; some kinds are famous for mimicking human speech
fact: Mynas are not one natural group: the name is used for any starling of the Indian subcontinent. The common myna is listed among the world's worst invasive species.

name: Mynah
hint: Asian starling relative famous as a talking cage bird; the hill species is a superb mimic
fact: Common mynas were introduced to many countries to control insects and are now listed among the world's worst invasive species.

name: Nandu
hint: Alternative name for the rhea, the large flightless bird of South America
fact: Male rheas incubate the eggs of several females in a single nest and then raise the chicks on their own.

name: Nene
hint: Hawaiian goose; the state bird of Hawaii
fact: Its name imitates its soft call. Nene feet are less webbed than other geese's, suiting rugged lava, and by 1952 only about 30 birds were left before captive breeding helped them recover.

name: Nest
hint: Structure a bird builds to hold its eggs
fact: The sociable weaver of southern Africa builds huge communal nests that can house over a hundred pairs and last for decades.

name: Nestling
hint: Young bird still too undeveloped to leave home; comes before the fledgling stage
fact: Songbird nestlings grow astonishingly fast, and many are ready to leave the nest less than two weeks after hatching.

name: Nide
hint: Old term for a brood of young pheasants
fact: Nide, from the Latin nidus, meaning nest, is an old term for a family of pheasants; it is also spelled nye.

name: Nighthawk
hint: American relative of the whip-poor-will; white wing bars flash as it hunts insects at dusk
fact: Despite the name, nighthawks are not hawks but nightjars. Male common nighthawks make a booming sound with their wings at the bottom of a courtship dive.

name: Nightingale
hint: Plain brown European songster famed in poetry for singing after dark
fact: Despite its fame, the common nightingale is a plain brown bird. Its powerful song is often heard at night, when unpaired males sing to attract migrating females.

name: Nightjar
hint: Camouflaged dusk flyer with a huge gape; the European species makes a churring song
fact: Nightjars hunt insects at dusk with wide, bristle-fringed mouths and spend the day motionless on the ground or a branch, camouflaged like dead leaves or bark.

name: Niltava
hint: Asian flycatcher; males are deep blue above with orange underparts
fact: Its name comes from 'niltau', the Nepali name for the rufous-bellied species.

name: Noddy
hint: Dark tropical tern with a pale cap, so tame that sailors could approach it easily
fact: Both parts of its scientific name, Anous stolidus, mean roughly 'stupid', because these fearless terns let sailors walk right up to them.

name: Nutcracker
hint: Crow relative of conifer forests that buries thousands of pine seeds and finds them again later
fact: Clark's nutcracker buries pine seeds in late summer and autumn and finds them months later by memory. Seeds it never retrieves help pine forests regrow.

name: Nuthatch
hint: Small, short-tailed tree-clinger that can climb down trunks headfirst
fact: Nuthatches are among the few birds that can walk headfirst down tree trunks. Their name comes from their habit of wedging nuts in bark and hacking them open.

name: Oilbird
hint: Nocturnal, fruit-eating cave dweller of South America that navigates by echolocation
fact: Its plump chicks were once boiled down for cooking and lamp oil, which gave it its name; it finds its way in dark caves by clicking.

name: Oology
hint: Study or collecting of birds' eggs
fact: Egg collecting was a popular Victorian hobby, but it harmed rare species and is now illegal in many countries, including the UK.

name: Openbill
hint: Stork whose mandibles meet only at the tip, leaving a gap for gripping snails
fact: The openbill's mandibles meet only at the tip, leaving a gap that helps it handle snails, its main food. The gap develops only as the bird matures.

name: Oriole
hint: Bright orange-and-black songbird that weaves a hanging, pouch-like nest; a Baltimore baseball team
fact: The name comes from Latin aureolus, 'golden'. American ones are relatives of blackbirds, unrelated to the Old World birds they were named after.

name: Ornithology
hint: Scientific study of birds
fact: The word comes from Greek ornis, bird; amateur birdwatchers add huge amounts of data to it through bird counts and surveys.

name: Oropendola
hint: Tropical American relative of orioles that weaves long hanging nests in colonies
fact: All oropendolas have tails that are at least partly bright yellow. Males are typically larger than females, and a colony may hang many woven nests from one tree.

name: Ortolan
hint: European bunting once eaten whole as a French delicacy
fact: Its name comes from Middle French hortolan, 'gardener'. Diners traditionally ate it whole with a napkin over their heads; it is now protected by French and EU law.

name: Osprey
hint: Fish-eating raptor that plunges feet-first into water; found on every continent but Antarctica
fact: Ospreys can swivel an outer toe backward to grip fish two toes in front and two behind, and they carry their catch head-first to cut drag.

name: Ostentation
hint: Collective noun for peacocks
fact: An ostentation of peacocks nods to the male's showy train of long covert feathers, which can carry well over a hundred shimmering eyespots.

name: Ostrich
hint: Tallest and heaviest living bird, a flightless runner of Africa
fact: Ostriches lay the largest eggs of any living bird and can sprint at about 70 km/h (43 mph); they don't really bury their heads in sand.

name: Ouzel
hint: Old word for a blackbird; the ring species has a white crescent on its chest
fact: The ring ouzel is an upland thrush of moors and mountains, and American dippers were once known as water ouzels.

name: Ovenbird
hint: Leaf-litter wood-warbler with an orange crown stripe; song sounds like 'teacher, teacher'
fact: The ovenbird is named for its domed ground nest with a side entrance, which resembles an old-fashioned outdoor oven.

name: Owlet
hint: Fluffy youngster of a nocturnal, hooting bird of prey
fact: Young owls often leave the nest before they can fly, clambering onto nearby branches as 'branchers' while their parents keep feeding them.

name: Oxpecker
hint: African starling-like bird that rides on buffalo and rhinos, eating ticks
fact: Oxpeckers eat ticks off large mammals but also peck at wounds to drink blood. The Swahili name for the red-billed species means 'the rhino's guard'.

name: Paddling
hint: Collective noun for ducks swimming on water
fact: Ducks swimming on water are a paddling, and some lists call them a team in flight, showing how the right word depends on what birds are doing.

name: Palmchat
hint: Streaky songbird found only on Hispaniola; national bird of the Dominican Republic
fact: The palmchat is the only member of its family. Flocks build huge shared stick nests in palm trees, in which each pair has its own chamber and entrance.

name: Pandemonium
hint: Collective noun for a noisy group of parrots
fact: Pandemonium, a fitting collective noun for loud parrots, was a word invented by the poet John Milton for his 1667 epic Paradise Lost.

name: Parakeet
hint: Small, long-tailed parrot; the budgie is the best-known pet example
fact: Feral rose-ringed parakeets, descended from escaped pets, now live wild in many European cities, including London.

name: Pardalote
hint: Tiny, brightly spotted Australian bird; some nest in tunnels dug into earth banks
fact: Pardalotes are tiny Australian birds whose name comes from a Greek word meaning 'spotted'. They feed mostly on lerps, sap-sucking insects on eucalyptus leaves.

name: Parliament
hint: Collective noun for owls
fact: This name for a group of owls may nod to their reputation for wisdom; C. S. Lewis called a chapter of The Silver Chair 'A Parliament of Owls'.

name: Parrot
hint: Hook-billed, often colourful bird famous for mimicking human speech
fact: Parrots have zygodactyl feet, with two toes pointing forward and two back, letting many species hold food up to their beak like a hand.

name: Parrotbill
hint: Small, long-tailed Asian songbird of reeds and bamboo with a short, stubby, seed-cracking beak
fact: Parrotbills are small Asian birds with stubby, parrot-like bills for eating seeds. Their family's only American member is the wrentit of western North America.

name: Parrotfinch
hint: Small green waxbill with red or blue head markings, from Southeast Asia to Pacific islands
fact: Parrotfinches are small, mostly green seed-eaters from Southeast Asia to Samoa, often with red rumps and blue or red faces. Several are kept as cage birds.

name: Parrotlet
hint: Tiny stubby-tailed hookbill of Central and South America; the Pacific species is a popular pet
fact: Parrotlets are the smallest parrots of the Americas. Studies of wild green-rumped parrotlets found that chicks learn their individual contact calls from their parents.

name: Partridge
hint: Plump Old World game bird; one famously perches in a pear tree in a Christmas carol
fact: Partridges are plump, ground-dwelling relatives of pheasants. Their chicks can leave the nest and peck for food themselves soon after hatching.

name: Parula
hint: Small blue-grey American wood-warbler with a yellow throat and a greenish back patch
fact: The northern parula often builds its nest inside hanging clumps of Spanish moss or beard lichen.

name: Passerine
hint: Perching bird; the huge order that includes sparrows and crows
fact: Perching birds make up more than half of all bird species; their name comes from Passer, the Latin for sparrow.

name: Pauraque
hint: Tropical American nightjar that reaches southern Texas; rests on the ground by day
fact: The pauraque is a nightjar found from southern Texas to Argentina. It hunts insects at night and rests camouflaged on the ground by day.

name: Peacock
hint: Male bird that fans a shimmering train of eyespot feathers to impress females
fact: A peacock's famous train isn't its tail: the long plumes grow from its back and are raised by the short, stiff tail underneath.

name: Peafowl
hint: Umbrella term for the species whose males display huge eyespotted trains
fact: The Indian species is India's national bird; strictly, the male is a peacock, the female a peahen and the chicks are peachicks.

name: Peahen
hint: Female of the bird whose males fan a giant tail of eyespots
fact: Peahens are mostly drab brown with a greenish lower neck, and scientists still debate how much the male's eyespot-covered train sways their choice of mate.

name: Peck
hint: Strike at or pick up food with the bill
fact: The phrase 'pecking order' comes from a 1920s study of hens, which set up a strict social ranking by jabbing at one another.

name: Pelican
hint: Large waterbird with a huge stretchy throat pouch for scooping up fish
fact: The Australian pelican has the longest bill of any living bird, reaching up to about 50 cm (20 in).

name: Pellet
hint: Bundle of fur and bones an owl coughs up
fact: Owls swallow prey whole and later cough up the fur and bones they cannot digest; scientists pick these apart to learn what owls eat.

name: Penguin
hint: Flightless tuxedoed seabird of the Southern Hemisphere that 'flies' underwater
fact: Emperor penguins can dive deeper than 500 m (1,600 ft) and stay underwater for more than 20 minutes.

name: Perch
hint: Sit on a branch or wire; also the branch itself
fact: Most birds have three toes forward and one back to grip branches, and the passerines, or 'perching birds', make up over half of all bird species.

name: Peregrine
hint: Falcon that tops 300 km/h in a hunting dive, the fastest animal on Earth
fact: In its hunting stoop the peregrine falcon can exceed 320 km/h (200 mph). Nearly wiped out by DDT in many regions, it recovered and now nests on skyscrapers.

name: Petrel
hint: Tube-nosed seabird; the storm variety patters over the waves as if walking on water
fact: The name is thought to honour Saint Peter, who walked on water, because some species patter their feet on the sea while feeding.

name: Pewee
hint: Small American flycatcher named after its plaintive whistled call
fact: Eastern and western wood-pewees look almost identical and are best told apart by voice; the eastern's slow, whistled 'pee-a-wee' gave these flycatchers their name.

name: Pewit
hint: Old name for the northern lapwing, echoing its wheezy call
fact: The northern lapwing, also called the green plover, performs tumbling display flights over farmland in spring.

name: Phainopepla
hint: Glossy black, crested desert songbird of the US Southwest that feasts on mistletoe berries
fact: The phainopepla's name means 'shining robe' in Greek, for the male's glossy black plumage. It eats many desert mistletoe berries and spreads the seeds.

name: Phalarope
hint: Shorebird that spins on water to stir up food; females are brighter than males
fact: Phalaropes reverse the usual roles: females are more brightly colored and court the males, which incubate the eggs and raise the chicks alone.

name: Pheasant
hint: Long-tailed game bird; common males have red face wattles and coppery plumage
fact: The common pheasant is native to Asia but was introduced across Europe and North America as a game bird. It is the state bird of South Dakota.

name: Phoebe
hint: American flycatcher that wags its tail and says its own name
fact: In 1804 John James Audubon tied silver threads to the legs of eastern phoebe nestlings, one of the first bird-banding experiments in North America.

name: Piculet
hint: Tiny, short-tailed woodpecker relative, mostly from South America
fact: Piculets are among the smallest woodpeckers, some under 10 cm long. They lack stiff tail feathers, so they perch on branches rather than climbing trunks.

name: Pigeon
hint: City-square bird descended from the rock dove; homing breeds carried wartime messages
fact: Homing pigeons can find their way home from hundreds of kilometres away, and messenger birds carried vital notes in both World Wars.

name: Piha
hint: Grey South American cotinga; the 'screaming' kind has one of the loudest bird calls
fact: The screaming piha is a plain grey bird, but its ear-splitting whistled call is one of the loudest of any bird and a signature sound of Amazonian rainforests.

name: Pinfeather
hint: New quill still wrapped in its waxy sheath and full of blood
fact: Growing pinfeathers carry a blood supply, so they are also called blood feathers; later, preening strips off the waxy sheath and the feather unfurls.

name: Pinion
hint: Outer part of a bird's wing bearing the flight feathers; also a small cogwheel
fact: To pinion a bird once meant clipping or binding its wing tip so it could not fly. The word later came to mean pinning a person's arms.

name: Pintail
hint: Elegant, slim dabbling duck; drakes have a chocolate head and very long central rear feathers
fact: Unusually for a duck that breeds across northern Europe, Asia and North America, the northern pintail has no geographical subspecies.

name: Pipit
hint: Small streaky brown ground bird resembling a lark; meadow and tree species breed in Britain
fact: Meadow pipits are among the cuckoo's most frequent hosts in Britain, often raising a chick far bigger than themselves.

name: Pishing
hint: Hissing noise birders make to draw curious small birds out of cover
fact: Pishing works because it sounds like the scolding calls of tits and chickadees, so other small birds come to see what the fuss is about.

name: Pitohui
hint: New Guinea songbird whose skin and feathers carry a nerve toxin
fact: The hooded pitohui is one of the few known poisonous birds: its skin and feathers carry batrachotoxins, the toxins of poison dart frogs, probably from beetles it eats.

name: Pitta
hint: Jewel-coloured, plump, short-tailed ground bird of forests in Asia, Africa and Australasia
fact: Nicknamed 'jewel thrushes' for their vivid plumage, pittas are not thrushes at all; they hop about forest floors hunting worms, snails and insects.

name: Plantcutter
hint: Finch-like South American cotinga with a serrated beak for slicing leaves
fact: Plantcutters are among the few birds that feed mainly on leaves, using fine saw-like serrations on their stubby bills to cut plant material.

name: Plover
hint: Short-billed, round-headed wader; the killdeer is one
fact: Many plovers fake a broken wing to lure predators away from their eggs, a trick called a distraction display.

name: Plumage
hint: A bird's whole coat of feathers
fact: Many birds change their look with the seasons. In summer 'eclipse' dress, male mallards lose their green heads and look like females for weeks.

name: Plume
hint: Long, showy feather, like those once taken from egrets for hats
fact: The 19th-century craze for egret and heron feathers on ladies' hats sparked some of the first bird protection societies and laws.

name: Pochard
hint: Diving duck; the European drake has a chestnut head, black chest and grey back
fact: The common pochard was reclassified as Vulnerable by the IUCN in 2015 after steep declines across much of its range.

name: Poorwill
hint: Western North American nightjar that can enter a hibernation-like state for weeks
fact: The common poorwill is the only bird known to go into torpor for weeks or months at a time, a state close to hibernation, often hidden in rock piles.

name: Potoo
hint: Nocturnal tropical American bird that poses as a broken branch by day; huge gape, eerie call
fact: By day potoos perch motionless on stumps, camouflaged as part of the branch, then hunt flying insects at night. Their haunting calls earned them the name poor-me-one.

name: Poult
hint: Young turkey or other game fowl
fact: Turkey poults leave the nest within a day of hatching and follow their mother as she forages, snapping up insects.

name: Poultry
hint: Domesticated birds kept for eggs or meat
fact: The chicken is the most populous poultry species, with over 20 billion alive at any one time, far more than any wild bird.

name: Pratincole
hint: Swallow-like shorebird with a forked tail that hunts insects on the wing
fact: Pratincoles are unusual waders that catch insects in flight like swallows. Their name comes from Latin for 'meadow dweller'.

name: Precocial
hint: Describes chicks that hatch with eyes open, ready to walk
fact: Chicks like those of ducks and chickens hatch covered in down with open eyes and can leave the nest within hours.

name: Preen
hint: Clean, oil and tidy feathers with the bill
fact: Birds preen every day, spreading oil from a gland at the base of the tail to keep their feathers clean, aligned and waterproof.

name: Prion
hint: Small blue-grey Southern Ocean petrel; some species sieve plankton through comb-like bill fringes
fact: Prions are also called whalebirds: some strain tiny crustaceans through fringed bills, rather like baleen whales. Their name comes from the Greek for 'saw'.

name: Ptarmigan
hint: Arctic and alpine grouse that turns white in winter and has feather-covered feet
fact: Ptarmigans have feathered feet that work like snowshoes, and most turn white in winter for camouflage. The willow species is the state bird of Alaska.

name: Pueo
hint: Hawaiian subspecies of the short-eared owl, revered as a guardian spirit
fact: The pueo is one of the best-known forms taken by aumakua, ancestral guardian spirits in Native Hawaiian culture. Unusually for an owl, it nests on the ground.

name: Puffbird
hint: Stout, big-headed Neotropical insect-eater with loose, fluffed-up plumage
fact: Puffbirds are named for their loose, fluffy plumage and short tails. They are relatives of the jacamars and often sit motionless for long periods waiting for prey.

name: Puffin
hint: Stubby seabird with a colourful triangular bill, nicknamed the 'clown of the sea'
fact: Puffins can carry a dozen or more small fish crosswise in their bill at once, using a rough tongue and spiny palate to hold them while they catch more.

name: Pukeko
hint: New Zealand name for the Australasian swamphen, a blue-purple rail with a red bill and forehead shield
fact: Pukeko often breed in groups, with several males and females sharing one nest and helping raise the chicks together.

name: Pullet
hint: Young hen, usually under a year old
fact: Pullets usually start laying at around five to six months old, and their first eggs are often noticeably small.

name: Pygostyle
hint: Fused tail vertebrae that anchor a bird's tail feathers
fact: This stubby fused bone replaced the long bony tail of early birds like Archaeopteryx; the fleshy lump it supports is nicknamed the parson's nose.

name: Pyrrhuloxia
hint: Grey-and-red 'desert cardinal' of the US Southwest and Mexico
fact: The pyrrhuloxia, or desert cardinal, is a close relative of the northern cardinal. Its name combines the genus names of bullfinches (Pyrrhula) and crossbills (Loxia).

name: Quack
hint: Classic call of a duck
fact: In mallards it is mainly the female that gives the loud, classic call; males make a quieter, raspier sound.

name: Quail
hint: Small plump ground bird hunted as game; its tiny speckled eggs are a delicacy
fact: In 1990 Japanese quail chicks hatched aboard the Mir space station, becoming the first birds ever born in space.

name: Quelea
hint: Small African weaver that gathers in flocks of millions and ravages crops
fact: The red-billed quelea is often called the world's most abundant wild bird, with a population that may exceed a billion.

name: Quetzal
hint: Emerald Central American bird with long tail plumes, sacred to the Maya and Aztecs
fact: The resplendent quetzal is Guatemala's national bird, and the country's currency, the quetzal, is named after it.

name: Quill
hint: Hollow shaft of a large feather, once cut into a writing pen
fact: For centuries most European writing was done with pens cut from goose or swan flight feathers, while fine crow feathers suited detailed drawing.

name: Raft
hint: Group of ducks, auks or other seabirds floating together
fact: Eiders, scoters and puffins gather in rafts on the sea, and some winter rafts of diving ducks number many thousands.

name: Rail
hint: Secretive, narrow-bodied marsh bird; its family also includes crakes and coots
fact: Rails often colonise remote islands and lose the power of flight. The Inaccessible Island rail of the South Atlantic is the smallest living flightless bird.

name: Raptor
hint: Bird of prey such as a hawk, eagle or owl
fact: Birds of prey have extraordinary eyesight, with far more light-sensing cells packed into part of the retina than humans have.

name: Ratite
hint: Flightless bird with a flat breastbone, like an ostrich or kiwi
fact: The group includes ostriches, emus, rheas, cassowaries and kiwis; its name comes from the Latin for 'raft', describing their keel-less breastbone.

name: Raven
hint: Large all-black corvid with a wedge-shaped tail and deep croak; famously kept at the Tower of London
fact: Common ravens are among the most intelligent birds, able to solve puzzles, plan ahead and even mimic human speech in captivity.

name: Razorbill
hint: Black-and-white Atlantic auk with a deep, blunt, white-striped beak
fact: The razorbill is the closest living relative of the extinct great auk. Chicks leap from cliff ledges into the sea before they can fly, and the father raises them at sea.

name: Rectrix
hint: Technical name for a single tail flight feather
fact: Rectrices, from the Latin for 'helmsman', are the tail feathers that steer and brake in flight. Many birds have twelve, arranged in pairs.

name: Redhead
hint: North American diving duck; drakes have a cinnamon face and crown, black chest and grey body
fact: Female redheads often lay eggs in other ducks' nests, including canvasbacks', as well as raising broods of their own.

name: Redpoll
hint: Small streaky Arctic finch with a crimson cap that visits winter feeders
fact: Redpolls survive frigid northern winters partly by storing seeds in a pouch in their throat to eat during long, cold nights.

name: Redshank
hint: Nervous, noisy Eurasian wader nicknamed 'warden of the marshes'; its legs are brightly colored
fact: The common redshank is a nervous, noisy wader, often the first to fly off with loud piping alarm calls that alert other birds to danger.

name: Redstart
hint: Songbird that constantly quivers its fiery orange tail
fact: The name redstart comes from Old English 'steort', meaning tail, for the bird's orange-red tail. Common redstarts often nest in tree holes.

name: Redwing
hint: Small European thrush with a cream eyebrow and rusty flanks, a winter visitor
fact: Redwings migrate at night; on autumn evenings in Britain their thin 'tseep' calls can often be heard overhead.

name: Reeve
hint: Female of the ruff, a Eurasian sandpiper
fact: Reeves are smaller and plainer than male ruffs, and a rare type of male even copies a reeve's plumage to slip unnoticed onto the males' display ground.

name: Remex
hint: Technical name for a single flight feather of the wing
fact: Remiges, from the Latin for 'rower', are the wing's flight feathers: primaries attach to the hand bones and secondaries to the forearm.

name: Rhea
hint: Large flightless South American bird, a relative of the ostrich and emu
fact: Male rheas do the parenting: several females lay eggs in one male's nest, and he incubates them and raises the chicks on his own.

name: Riflebird
hint: Velvet-black paradise species of Australia and New Guinea named after an army uniform
fact: Riflebirds are birds-of-paradise named for their velvety black plumage, likened to the uniform of the British Rifle Brigade.

name: Rifleman
hint: New Zealand's tiniest endemic songbird, a green wren-like insect-eater
fact: The rifleman is New Zealand's smallest endemic bird. It belongs to an ancient family of New Zealand wrens that are not related to true wrens.

name: Ringing
hint: Fitting a numbered leg band to track wild birds
fact: Bird ringing, or banding, reveals lifespans: a Laysan albatross named Wisdom, first ringed in 1956, was still breeding in her 70s.

name: Roadrunner
hint: Speedy ground cuckoo of the US Southwest that eats rattlesnakes; a cartoon star
fact: Greater roadrunners can sprint at about 32 km/h (20 mph) and are quick enough to catch and eat rattlesnakes. They belong to the cuckoo family.

name: Robin
hint: Red-breasted garden songbird; the European one is a Christmas card favourite
fact: European robins are fiercely territorial and sing through winter; the American 'robin' is a larger thrush named by settlers for its similar red breast.

name: Rockjumper
hint: Black-throated, rufous-bellied songbird of southern African mountain slopes; its family has two species
fact: Rockjumpers are found only in southern Africa and form their own family, Chaetopidae. They hop and run over rocky mountain slopes more than they fly.

name: Roller
hint: Jay-sized, brilliantly coloured Old World bird; the lilac-breasted kind is a safari favourite
fact: Rollers are named for their acrobatic display flights, in which they twist and tumble through the air.

name: Rook
hint: Gregarious corvid with a bare whitish face; shares its name with a chess piece
fact: Rooks nest together in noisy treetop colonies called rookeries. In experiments, captive rooks have used and even shaped tools to solve puzzles.

name: Rookery
hint: Noisy treetop nesting colony of crow-family birds, or of penguins or seals
fact: Rooks nest in noisy treetop colonies, and the name for these was later extended to breeding colonies of penguins and seals.

name: Roost
hint: Settle down to sleep, often in a big group
fact: Winter gatherings of European starlings can top a million birds, all flying in at dusk to sleep together in reedbeds or woods.

name: Rooster
hint: Adult male chicken
fact: Roosters crow mainly around dawn thanks to an internal body clock, and the top-ranking male in a flock usually crows first.

name: Rosefinch
hint: Pinkish-red Eurasian seed-eater, with most of its species in the Himalayas and China
fact: Most rosefinches live in the Sino-Himalayan mountains. The common rosefinch's song is often transcribed as 'pleased to meet you'.

name: Rosella
hint: Colourful Australian parrot with a scalloped back and bright cheek patches
fact: The name comes from Rose Hill (now Parramatta, Sydney), where early settlers first encountered the eastern species.

name: Ruff
hint: Sandpiper whose breeding males grow a showy feather collar; females are reeves
fact: Male ruffs come in three types: territorial 'independents', satellite males, and rare 'faeders' that look like females and sneak matings at the lek.

name: Ruru
hint: Maori name for New Zealand's small brown owl, the morepork
fact: The ruru, or morepork, is named for its call, which sounds like 'more-pork'. It is New Zealand's only surviving native owl.

name: Saker
hint: Large falcon of Central Asian steppes, highly prized by Arab falconers
fact: Sakers have been prized by falconers for centuries and can reach about 150 km/h in level flight. In 2012 Mongolia made the saker falcon its national bird.

name: Saltator
hint: Thick-billed Neotropical tanager whose name is Latin for 'dancer'
fact: Saltators are thick-billed tanagers of Central and South America. They were placed in the cardinal family until genetic studies moved them.

name: Sanderling
hint: Pale little shorebird that sprints back and forth chasing retreating waves
fact: Sanderlings breed in the high Arctic yet winter on beaches worldwide. Unlike most sandpipers, they lack a hind toe.

name: Sandgrouse
hint: Dry-country ground bird whose males soak their belly feathers to carry water to their chicks
fact: Male sandgrouse soak their specially adapted belly feathers at waterholes, then fly back, sometimes many kilometers, so their chicks can drink from them.

name: Sandpiper
hint: Small shorebird that probes wet mud with a slender beak; many make epic migrations
fact: The sandpiper family, Scolopacidae, also includes woodcocks, curlews and snipes. One member, the bar-tailed godwit, flies nonstop for over 11,000 km.

name: Sapsucker
hint: North American woodpecker that drills neat rows of wells in bark to feed on the sugary fluid
fact: Sapsuckers drill rows of small holes in trees and return to lick up the sap and trapped insects. Hummingbirds often feed at these sap wells too.

name: Scarecrow
hint: Straw figure put in fields to frighten birds away
fact: Birds soon learn that a motionless scarecrow is harmless, so it works best when moved often or given flapping, shiny or noisy parts.

name: Scaup
hint: Diving duck with a blue-grey bill and black-and-white drake; greater and lesser species
fact: Its name may come from 'scalp', an old word for the mussel beds where these diving ducks feed in winter.

name: Scoter
hint: Dark sea duck; drakes are mostly black with a knobbed or colourful bill
fact: Scoters dive for mussels and clams and swallow them whole, crushing the shells in their powerful gizzard.

name: Scrape
hint: Simple shallow hollow in the ground used as a nest
fact: Many shorebirds, terns and falcons lay their eggs in a scrape, a shallow dip in the ground or on a cliff ledge, sometimes lined with pebbles.

name: Screamer
hint: Goose-sized South American waterbird with sharp spurs on its wings and a loud honking call
fact: Screamers are related to ducks and geese but look more like turkeys. They have two sharp spurs on each wing and many air sacs beneath the skin.

name: Screech
hint: Harsh, shrill cry, like that of a barn owl
fact: Barn owls don't hoot; they give a long, harsh shriek, which is why they were once called screech owls in Britain.

name: Scrubbird
hint: Secretive Australian ground-dweller; one species was thought extinct until its 1961 rediscovery
fact: The noisy scrubbird was thought to be extinct until it was rediscovered in Western Australia in 1961. Scrubbirds are ancient relatives of the lyrebirds.

name: Scrubfowl
hint: Big-footed, mound-building megapode of Southeast Asia, northern Australia and Pacific islands
fact: Scrubfowl bury their eggs in huge mounds of rotting vegetation, and the male adds or removes material to regulate the heat until the chicks hatch.

name: Seabird
hint: Puffin, albatross or other species that lives mostly over the ocean
fact: Many ocean birds can drink seawater, getting rid of the extra salt through special glands above their eyes.

name: Seagull
hint: Popular, unscientific name for a noisy coastal bird that snatches chips
fact: Birders prefer plain 'gull', since many gulls live and breed far inland. An older name for gulls is 'mew', which, like 'gull', imitates their calls.

name: Seedeater
hint: Small conical-billed Neotropical tanager, related to Darwin's finches
fact: Many seedeaters of the Americas are small tanagers closely related to Darwin's finches. Their stout, conical bills are built for cracking grass seeds.

name: Seedsnipe
hint: Plump, plant-eating South American shorebird of the Andes and Patagonia
fact: Seedsnipes are unusual shorebirds that eat plants instead of animals. They live in the Andes and Patagonia and look more like partridges than snipes.

name: Seriema
hint: Long-legged South American bird that kills prey by beating it on the ground
fact: Seriemas have a raised, sickle-like claw on each foot and are the closest living relatives of the extinct 'terror birds'.

name: Serin
hint: Small streaky yellow European finch, a close cousin of the canary
fact: The European serin spread north from the Mediterranean across much of Europe during the 19th and 20th centuries.

name: Shama
hint: Long-tailed Asian songbird; the white-rumped species is a famed songster
fact: White-rumped shamas are prized for their rich, varied songs, and their popularity as cage birds led to introductions elsewhere, including Hawaii in the 20th century.

name: Sharpbill
hint: Small tropical American fruit-eater with a pointed beak and a hidden orange crest
fact: The sharpbill is the only member of its family, Oxyruncidae. It lives in the canopy of wet forests and has an orange crest it can raise.

name: Shearwater
hint: Long-winged tube-nosed seabird that glides low, seeming to slice the wave tops
fact: Sooty shearwaters make one of the longest animal migrations known: tracked birds from New Zealand looped around the whole Pacific, flying about 64,000 km.

name: Sheathbill
hint: White, pigeon-like Antarctic scavenger with a horny plate over its beak base
fact: Sheathbills are the only bird family endemic to the Antarctic region as breeders, and the only Antarctic birds without webbed feet. They scavenge around penguin colonies.

name: Shelduck
hint: Large, goose-like waterfowl; the common species is white with a chestnut breast band and red bill
fact: Common shelducks often nest in rabbit burrows. After breeding, many fly to the Wadden Sea to moult together in huge flocks.

name: Shikra
hint: Small hawk of Africa and Asia, also called the little banded goshawk
fact: Drongos imitate the shikra's sharp two-note call, and the common hawk-cuckoo looks so much like it that the two are easily confused.

name: Shoebill
hint: Huge grey African swamp bird with a massive, broad, hook-tipped beak; hunts lungfish
fact: The shoebill can stand motionless for long periods before lunging at prey such as lungfish. Its enormous bill also earns it the name whale-headed stork.

name: Shorebird
hint: North American term for waders like plovers and sandpipers
fact: Red knots time their spring migration to feast on horseshoe crab eggs in Delaware Bay, fattening up fast for the flight to the Arctic.

name: Shoveler
hint: Dabbling duck with an oversized, spade-shaped beak for filtering food from water
fact: The northern shoveler's huge bill has comb-like edges that strain tiny animals and seeds from water. Groups often feed while swimming in tight circles.

name: Shrike
hint: Hook-billed songbird that impales prey on thorns; the 'butcher bird'
fact: Shrikes spike prey on thorns or barbed wire to make 'larders' that store food and help males attract mates; the genus name Lanius means 'butcher'.

name: Sibia
hint: Long-tailed Asian babbler of the genus Heterophasia, found in hill forests
fact: The rufous species is a noisy, familiar bird of Himalayan hill forests, often seen in lively flocks.

name: Siege
hint: Collective noun for herons
fact: A siege of herons may come from the way a heron stands motionless at the water's edge, as if laying siege to the fish in the shallows.

name: Silvereye
hint: Tiny olive songbird of Australia and New Zealand with a pale spectacle-like ring; Maori name tauhou
fact: The silvereye arrived in New Zealand in large numbers in 1856, probably blown across from Australia. Its Maori name, tauhou, means 'stranger'.

name: Siskin
hint: Small yellow-green finch that dangles upside down to pick seeds from alder and birch
fact: Siskins feed acrobatically like tits and often visit garden feeders in winter; the pine siskin is their North American relative.

name: Sittella
hint: Small Australasian bark-forager that climbs headfirst down branches like a nuthatch
fact: Sittellas look and behave like nuthatches but belong to their own Australasian family, Neosittidae, an example of convergent evolution.

name: Skein
hint: Group of geese flying in a V or line
fact: A skein is a flock of geese in flight, often in a V formation; on the ground or water the same birds are called a gaggle.

name: Skimmer
hint: Tern-like waterbird whose lower bill is longer than the upper; once called the scissorbill
fact: Skimmers fly low with the tip of their lower bill slicing through the water, snapping it shut the instant it touches a fish.

name: Skua
hint: Piratical seabird that chases others to steal their food; jaeger in North America
fact: Skuas often chase other seabirds until they drop or cough up their catch. They range so far south that they have even been sighted at the South Pole.

name: Skylark
hint: Streaky brown songbird of open fields that sings nonstop while hovering high overhead
fact: Its soaring song inspired Shelley's poem 'To a Skylark' and Vaughan Williams's much-loved music 'The Lark Ascending'.

name: Smew
hint: Small diving duck; the drake is white with black 'cracked ice' markings
fact: The smew is the only living member of its genus, Mergellus. It nests in tree holes, often old woodpecker holes, in the forests of northern Europe and Asia.

name: Snipe
hint: Long-billed, camouflaged marsh wader with a zigzag escape flight; also the quarry of a classic prank hunt
fact: The word 'sniper' comes from hunters skilled enough to shoot this zigzagging bird; males also 'drum' by vibrating their tail feathers in dives.

name: Snood
hint: Fleshy flap dangling over a male turkey's beak
fact: A tom turkey's snood can lengthen and flush red within moments during display, and studies suggest hens prefer males with longer ones.

name: Snowcock
hint: Large mountain partridge of the Himalayas and Caucasus; one species lives wild in Nevada
fact: Snowcocks live high in the mountains of Eurasia. The Himalayan snowcock was introduced to Nevada in the 1960s and still lives in the Ruby Mountains.

name: Snowfinch
hint: Sparrow relative of high mountains from the Pyrenees to Tibet, with white wing patches
fact: Snowfinches are sparrow relatives of high mountains from the Pyrenees to Tibet. Some Tibetan species nest in burrows dug by pikas, small relatives of rabbits.

name: Soar
hint: Fly high without flapping, riding rising air
fact: Vultures and eagles circle upward on thermals, columns of rising warm air, then glide off to find the next one, barely flapping for hours.

name: Songbird
hint: Thrush, finch or other oscine perching species with a complex voice box
fact: Songbirds probably first evolved in Australia around 50 million years ago, and the group surprisingly includes crows and ravens despite their harsh calls.

name: Sora
hint: Small, yellow-billed North American crake known for a descending whinny
fact: The sora is far more often heard than seen. Despite its small size and weak-looking flight, it migrates as far as northern South America.

name: Sparrow
hint: Small brown-and-grey seed-eater; the house kind lives alongside people worldwide
fact: Carried by people to Australasia, Africa and the Americas, the house sparrow has become the most widely distributed wild bird on Earth.

name: Sparrowhawk
hint: Small Eurasian woodland raptor that ambushes songbirds; females are far bigger than males
fact: The female Eurasian sparrowhawk is up to 25% larger than the male, one of the greatest size differences between the sexes in any bird species.

name: Speculum
hint: Glossy coloured patch on a duck's wing
fact: Named from the Latin for 'mirror', a mallard's speculum is iridescent purple-blue edged with white; the shimmer comes from feather structure, not pigment.

name: Spinebill
hint: Small Australian honeyeater with a very long, thin, down-curved beak
fact: Australia's two spinebill species sip nectar with long, needle-like bills. Genetic studies show they branched off before all other honeyeaters.

name: Spink
hint: Dialect name for the chaffinch, echoing its sharp call note
fact: Male chaffinches have regional song dialects, and young birds learn their songs from neighbours in their first spring.

name: Spoonbill
hint: Wading bird that sweeps a flat, paddle-tipped beak side to side through shallow water
fact: Spoonbills feed by sweeping their open bills through water and snapping them shut on prey. The roseate spoonbill of the Americas is pink, like a flamingo.

name: Spur
hint: Bony spike on the back of a rooster's or pheasant's leg
fact: Roosters and male pheasants use their leg spurs as weapons against rivals, and turkey hunters judge a gobbler's age by the length of his.

name: Spurfowl
hint: African partridge-like game bird named for the sharp spikes on males' legs
fact: Spurfowl are partridge-like game birds of Africa. They are strictly monogamous and get most of their food by digging, living largely on roots, tubers and seeds.

name: Squab
hint: Young pigeon, also served as a delicacy
fact: Young pigeons are fed crop milk by both parents and grow so fast that they reach nearly adult weight in about a month.

name: Squawk
hint: Loud, harsh cry, like a parrot's
fact: Wild parrots make loud, harsh calls to keep in touch with their flock mates as they fly through dense forest.

name: Starling
hint: Glossy, speckled songbird famous for swirling murmuration flocks and mimicking sounds
fact: North America's many millions of common starlings descend from about 100 birds released in New York's Central Park in 1890 and 1891.

name: Stilt
hint: Black-and-white wader with extremely long pink legs and a needle-thin bill
fact: Relative to its body size, the black-winged stilt has some of the longest legs of any bird.

name: Stint
hint: Tiny sandpiper; little and Temminck's are species seen on migration
fact: The little stint weighs only about 25 grams, yet it migrates each year between Arctic breeding grounds in Europe and Asia and winter homes in Africa and South Asia.

name: Stitchbird
hint: Rare New Zealand nectar-feeder, the hihi, placed in a family all its own
fact: The stitchbird, or hihi, is the only member of its family. It once survived only on Little Barrier Island but has been reintroduced to several other sanctuaries.

name: Stonechat
hint: Small songbird that perches on gorse tops; males have a black head, white neck patch and orange breast
fact: The stonechat is named for its alarm call, which sounds like two stones being tapped together.

name: Stoop
hint: A falcon's steep, high-speed dive onto prey
fact: A peregrine falcon diving on prey can exceed 300 km/h, making it the fastest animal on Earth.

name: Stork
hint: Tall wader with a long stout bill; in folklore it delivers newborn babies
fact: In 1822 a white stork arrived in Germany with an African spear through its neck, helping prove that birds migrate rather than hibernate.

name: Sugarbird
hint: Long-tailed southern African nectar-feeder closely tied to protea flowers
fact: Sugarbirds live only in southern Africa and feed on nectar from protea flowers. The male Cape sugarbird's tail can be much longer than its body.

name: Sunbird
hint: Tiny, iridescent, curve-billed nectar-feeder of Africa and Asia
fact: Sunbirds look like hummingbirds but are unrelated; unlike hummingbirds, they usually perch rather than hover while sipping nectar.

name: Sunbittern
hint: Tropical American wader that flashes eye-like patterns on its spread wings
fact: When threatened, the sunbittern spreads its wings to reveal large eye-like patterns. Its closest living relative is the kagu of New Caledonia.

name: Sungrebe
hint: Tropical American finfoot; males carry chicks in skin pockets under their wings
fact: The male sungrebe has pockets of skin under its wings in which it can carry its chicks, even in flight, a trait almost unique among birds.

name: Supercilium
hint: Pale 'eyebrow' stripe running above a bird's eye
fact: Birders use it to tell look-alikes apart, such as the dusky warbler and Radde's warbler. The word is simply Latin for 'eyebrow'.

name: Surfbird
hint: Stocky Pacific coast wader that feeds on wave-splashed rocks; breeds on Alaskan tundra
fact: Surfbirds breed on rocky mountain tundra in Alaska and Yukon, then winter along the Pacific coast of the Americas, feeding on wave-battered rocks.

name: Swallow
hint: Fork-tailed aerial insect-catcher whose spring return heralds summer
fact: The barn swallow is the world's most widespread swallow, breeding across the Northern Hemisphere and wintering as far south as Argentina.

name: Swamphen
hint: Big purple-blue rail with a red bill and forehead shield; New Zealand's version is the pukeko
fact: Swamphens are large rails of the genus Porphyrio. Their relative the takahe of New Zealand was thought extinct until it was rediscovered in 1948.

name: Swan
hint: Large, long-necked waterfowl; its young are called cygnets
fact: In Britain the Crown can claim unmarked mute swans on open water, and each summer the 'Swan Upping' ceremony counts the swans on the River Thames.

name: Swift
hint: Scythe-winged aerial bird that eats, drinks and even sleeps on the wing
fact: Common swifts can stay airborne for around ten months at a time, landing only when they are ready to nest and breed.

name: Swiftlet
hint: Small cave-roosting aerial insect-eater; some build nests of hardened saliva used in soup
fact: Some swiftlets navigate dark caves using echolocation clicks. The edible-nest swiftlet builds its nest from saliva, the key ingredient in costly bird's nest soup.

name: Swoop
hint: Dive down suddenly through the air, as a hawk onto prey
fact: In Australia, protective magpies famously dive at walkers and cyclists who come too near their nests each spring.

name: Syrinx
hint: A bird's voice box, found where the windpipe splits in two
fact: Because the syrinx sits where the windpipe divides, some songbirds can control each side separately and sing two different notes at once.

name: Tailorbird
hint: Small Asian warbler that stitches leaves together to hold its nest
fact: Tailorbirds pierce holes along leaf edges and 'sew' the leaves together with plant fiber or spider silk to make a cradle for their nest.

name: Takahe
hint: Chunky, flightless purple-blue rail of New Zealand's mountains
fact: Presumed extinct after 1898, the takahe was dramatically rediscovered in 1948 in New Zealand's remote Murchison Mountains.

name: Talon
hint: Hooked, needle-sharp claw of an eagle, hawk or owl
fact: Hawks, eagles and owls kill with their feet rather than their beaks. An osprey's curved claws and spiny-soled toes let it grip slippery fish.

name: Tanager
hint: Brightly coloured American songbird; the scarlet kind has jet-black wings
fact: Darwin's finches of the Galapagos actually belong to the tanager family, the second-largest bird family, making up about 4% of all bird species.

name: Tapaculo
hint: Small, secretive South American ground bird that often cocks its tail upright
fact: Tapaculos are secretive, mouse-like birds and weak fliers. Many species look almost identical and are best identified by song.

name: Teal
hint: Small dabbling duck that gives its name to a blue-green colour
fact: The colour teal is named after the blue-green stripe on this little duck's head. Outside the breeding season teal are very sociable and gather in large flocks.

name: Tern
hint: Slender, fork-tailed seabird; the Arctic species makes a record migration
fact: The Arctic tern flies from Arctic breeding grounds to Antarctic waters and back every year, one of the longest migrations of any animal, so it sees two summers a year.

name: Tesia
hint: Tiny, almost tailless Asian bush warbler that hops on the forest floor
fact: These tiny, nearly tailless warblers have surprisingly loud, explosive songs for their size.

name: Thornbill
hint: Tiny Australian warbler-like songbird, such as the yellow-rumped or brown species
fact: Brown thornbills mimic other birds' hawk alarm calls, which can scare predators such as currawongs away from their nests.

name: Thrasher
hint: Long-tailed American mimic with a curved bill; the brown species has a huge song repertoire
fact: The brown thrasher has over 1,000 song types, one of the largest repertoires of any bird. It is the state bird of Georgia.

name: Thrush
hint: Songbird family that includes the American robin, the blackbird and the bluebirds
fact: The wood thrush can sing two notes at once, using the two sides of its voice box (syrinx) independently to make its flute-like song.

name: Tiercel
hint: Male falcon or hawk in falconry
fact: The name comes from an Old French word meaning 'third', often explained by the male being about a third smaller than the female.

name: Tinamou
hint: Ground-dwelling Latin American bird related to rheas that lays shiny eggs
fact: Tinamous lay some of the glossiest eggs of any bird, often turquoise or purple, and the males incubate them.

name: Tinkerbird
hint: Tiny African barbet whose monotonous call sounds like a hammer tapping metal
fact: Tinkerbirds are tiny African barbets named for their repetitive, metallic calls, likened to a tinker hammering on metal.

name: Titmouse
hint: Small grey crested North American songbird related to chickadees
fact: Tufted titmice sometimes pluck hair from live mammals to line their nests, a behavior called kleptotrichy. The 'mouse' in the name comes from an old word for a small bird.

name: Tody
hint: Tiny green Caribbean bird with a red throat, related to kingfishers
fact: The five living species of this family are found only on Caribbean islands. These tiny birds dig their nesting burrows into earth banks.

name: Tomtit
hint: Small black-and-white New Zealand robin with a white or yellow breast
fact: The North Island tomtit is the miromiro in Maori, while in Britain 'tomtit' is an old folk name for the blue tit.

name: Toucan
hint: Tropical American bird with an enormous, brightly coloured bill
fact: A toucan's giant bill is surprisingly light, a keratin shell over a honeycomb of bone, and it helps the bird shed excess body heat.

name: Toucanet
hint: Small big-billed fruit-eater of Neotropical forests, like the mostly green emerald species
fact: Toucanets are small members of the toucan family. The northern emerald toucanet is mostly green, which helps it blend into mountain cloud forests.

name: Towhee
hint: Large, long-tailed sparrow that scratches leaf litter with a two-footed backward hop
fact: The eastern towhee's name imitates its call, and its song is often remembered as 'drink-your-teeeea!'

name: Tragopan
hint: Asian mountain 'horned pheasant' whose males inflate a colorful throat lappet
fact: Male tragopans display by inflating a brightly colored throat lappet and raising fleshy horns. Unusually for their family, they nest in trees.

name: Treecreeper
hint: Small bark-brown songbird that spirals up trunks, probing with a thin curved beak
fact: Treecreepers climb up trunks in spirals, propped on stiff tail feathers, then fly down to the base of the next tree and start again.

name: Treepie
hint: Long-tailed Asian member of the crow family, often seen in forests and gardens
fact: Treepies are long-tailed Asian relatives of crows and jays that resemble magpies; the rufous treepie is a common garden bird in India.

name: Treeswift
hint: Crested aerial insect-eater of India to New Guinea that, unlike its close relatives, perches on branches
fact: Unlike true swifts, treeswifts perch on branches. They lay a single egg in a tiny nest glued to the side of a branch.

name: Trill
hint: Rapidly repeated run of notes in birdsong
fact: Many songbirds, such as dark-eyed juncos and chipping sparrows, sing rapid trills made of one note repeated many times a second.

name: Trogon
hint: Colourful tropical bird with a long square tail; the quetzal belongs to its family
fact: Its family has a foot layout found in no other birds: the first and second toes point backward and the third and fourth point forward.

name: Tropicbird
hint: White ocean flier of warm seas with two very long central tail streamers
fact: Tropicbirds' legs are set so far back that they can barely walk on land, so they nest on cliffs and ledges where they can launch easily into flight.

name: Trumpeter
hint: Hunched, chicken-sized Amazon forest bird named for the males' loud threat call
fact: Trumpeters are hunched, long-legged birds of Amazon forests that live in groups. They feed largely on fallen fruit, especially fruit knocked down by monkeys.

name: Turaco
hint: Crested African fruit-eater with red and green feathers coloured by unique pigments
fact: Turaco feathers get their vivid colours from unusual pigments: a green one called turacoverdin and a copper-containing red called turacin.

name: Turca
hint: Large, ground-dwelling Chilean tapaculo with a bold white moustache stripe
fact: Found only in Chile, this big tapaculo mostly runs rather than flies, and it digs its nest burrow into steep hillsides.

name: Turkey
hint: Large North American game bird with a fleshy wattle; the star of Thanksgiving dinner
fact: Unlike most farm breeds, wild turkeys can fly and roost in trees at night, and a male's bare head can shift between red, white and blue.

name: Turnstone
hint: Stocky Arctic-breeding shorebird with a short wedge-shaped bill; the ruddy species has orange legs
fact: Ruddy turnstones breed in the Arctic and winter on coasts worldwide, using short, wedge-shaped bills to flip over stones, shells and seaweed.

name: Tweet
hint: Thin, high call of a small bird, later a social media post
fact: Long before it meant a social media post, this was simply the word imitating a small bird's thin call, recorded in English since the 1800s.

name: Twitcher
hint: British slang for a birder who rushes off to see rarities
fact: Twitchers will travel hundreds of miles at short notice to see a rare vagrant, and missing one is called 'dipping'.

name: Twite
hint: Small brown upland finch, a close relative of the linnet, with a yellow bill in winter
fact: Its name imitates its nasal call, it was once nicknamed the 'mountain linnet', and its scientific name flavirostris means 'yellow-billed'.

name: Unkindness
hint: Collective noun for ravens
fact: An unkindness of ravens dates to the 15th century, probably from an old belief that ravens neglected their young; they are devoted parents.

name: Vagrant
hint: Bird found far outside its normal range
fact: Storms can blow birds thousands of kilometres off course, and a single lost American songbird in Britain can draw hundreds of birdwatchers.

name: Vanga
hint: Madagascan songbird family whose members evolved a spectacular variety of bill shapes
fact: Madagascar's vangas are a textbook adaptive radiation, with bills ranging from the sicklebill's long curve to the helmet vanga's massive blue beak.

name: Veery
hint: North American thrush whose flute-like song spirals downward
fact: Also called Wilson's thrush after ornithologist Alexander Wilson, the veery probably gets its English name from an imitation of its own call.

name: Verdin
hint: Tiny grey desert songbird with a yellow face that builds a ball-shaped thorny nest
fact: Verdins build bulky, round nests of thorny twigs with a side entrance, using them to raise young and to roost in on cold desert nights.

name: Vireo
hint: Small olive-green American songbird; the red-eyed species sings tirelessly all day
fact: One red-eyed vireo was once counted singing over 20,000 songs in a single day, and its nonstop, sermon-like phrases earned it the nickname 'preacher bird'.

name: Vulture
hint: Bald-headed scavenger that soars on thermals searching for carcasses
fact: A group of these birds circling in flight is called a 'kettle', a group resting in trees is a 'committee', and a group feeding is a 'wake'.

name: Waddle
hint: Group of penguins walking on land
fact: A group of penguins on land is sometimes called a waddle, after their rocking walk; the same birds at sea may be called a raft.

name: Wader
hint: Long-legged shorebird such as a sandpiper or curlew
fact: Waders probe mud with bills of different lengths and shapes, so many species can share one shore, each reaching different prey.

name: Wagtail
hint: Slim pied, grey or yellow songbird that runs after insects, constantly bobbing its rear
fact: Wagtails pump their tails almost nonstop, and the white wagtail is the national bird of Latvia.

name: Wallcreeper
hint: Grey Eurasian mountain songbird with crimson wings that flutters over sheer rock faces
fact: The wallcreeper is the only living member of its family. It clings to cliffs in Eurasian mountains, flicking open its crimson wings like a butterfly.

name: Warble
hint: Sing with melodious runs and quavers
fact: The word comes from an Old French term for a melody, and gave its name to warblers, a large group of small, often musical songbirds.

name: Warbler
hint: Small, busy insect-eating songbird; many North American kinds are bright yellow
fact: This name isn't one family: it covers small, vocal, insect-eating songbirds from several unrelated groups, such as the colourful New World wood-warblers.

name: Waterfowl
hint: Ducks, geese and swans taken together
fact: These birds have waterproof feathers and webbed feet, and many species migrate thousands of kilometres between breeding and wintering grounds.

name: Waterthrush
hint: Streaky, tail-bobbing American wood-warbler of streams and swamps
fact: Waterthrushes are not thrushes but New World warblers. Both species walk along streams and swamps, bobbing their tails like sandpipers.

name: Wattle
hint: Fleshy flap hanging under a chicken's or turkey's chin
fact: Wattles help chickens shed heat, and they can be so striking they name species: the southern cassowary is also called the double-wattled cassowary.

name: Wattlebird
hint: Large Australian honeyeater; some species have fleshy flaps hanging from the cheeks
fact: Wattlebirds are large honeyeaters found only in Australia. Some species have fleshy wattles on their cheeks, and the red wattlebird is common in city gardens.

name: Waxbill
hint: Tiny African finch with a glossy scarlet beak, popular in aviaries
fact: Named for beaks that look like red sealing wax, waxbills belong to a family that also includes the zebra finch and the Gouldian finch.

name: Waxwing
hint: Silky, crested songbird that gorges on berries; flight feathers have bright red tips
fact: Waxwings sometimes become tipsy from fermented berries, and courting pairs pass a berry back and forth between their bills.

name: Weaver
hint: African finch-like bird that knots grass into elaborate hanging nests
fact: Many male weavers tie real knots with their bills, and females inspect a male's nest before choosing him as a mate.

name: Weaverbird
hint: Small African or Asian finch-like songster whose male knots grass into intricate hanging nests
fact: Male weaverbirds knot strips of grass into elaborate hanging nests. The sociable weaver's communal nests are among the largest built by any bird, housing over 100 pairs.

name: Wedge
hint: Collective noun for swans or geese flying in a V
fact: Swans or geese flying in a V are a wedge; the formation is thought to save energy as each bird rides rising air off the wingtip ahead.

name: Weebill
hint: Australia's smallest bird, a tiny yellowish, warbler-like songbird of eucalypt woodland
fact: At about 8-9 cm long, the weebill is Australia's smallest bird, named for its short, stubby beak.

name: Weka
hint: Bold, chicken-sized flightless rail of New Zealand, also called the woodhen
fact: Weka are famously curious: they poke around houses and campsites for food scraps and anything portable, and are known to make off with shiny objects.

name: Whaup
hint: Scots name for the curlew, from its wild call
fact: This very large wader probes mud with its long, down-curved bill, and its bubbling spring call is a classic moorland sound.

name: Wheatear
hint: Small chat with a bold white rump; the northern species migrates from the Arctic to Africa
fact: Tracking shows the northern wheatear makes one of the longest migrations of any songbird, up to 30,000 km a year between sub-Saharan Africa and the Arctic.

name: Whimbrel
hint: Brown subarctic-breeding wader with a down-curved bill and striped crown; a small curlew
fact: Whimbrels are small curlews. Their rippling call of about seven whistled notes earned them the old folk name 'seven whistler'.

name: Whinchat
hint: Small streaky songbird of meadows with a bold pale eyebrow; perches on fence posts
fact: The whinchat breeds in Europe and western Asia and winters in central Africa. 'Whin' is an old word for gorse, a shrub it likes to perch on.

name: Whio
hint: New Zealand's blue duck of fast mountain rivers; its name echoes the male's whistle
fact: The whio, or blue duck, lives on fast-flowing mountain rivers and is pictured on the back of New Zealand's $10 banknote.

name: Whipbird
hint: Crested olive Australian songster; the male's call ends in a sharp crack like a stockman's lash
fact: The eastern whipbird's whip-crack song is a familiar sound in east Australian forests, and the female often answers the male's call almost instantly in a duet.

name: Whitethroat
hint: Scratchy-voiced Old World hedgerow warbler; males sing in a jerky, dancing song flight
fact: The common whitethroat winters in Africa's Sahel. Britain's breeding population crashed around 1969 after a severe drought there.

name: Whydah
hint: African finch whose breeding males grow extremely long tail streamers
fact: Whydahs are brood parasites of waxbills, and their chicks mimic the host chicks' mouth markings so they get fed.

name: Widowbird
hint: African weaver whose breeding males sport an extremely long black tail
fact: In a classic 1982 experiment, male long-tailed widowbirds given artificially lengthened tails attracted more mates, showing that females prefer long tails.

name: Wigeon
hint: Short-billed dabbling duck whose drake gives a clear whistling 'whee-oo'
fact: Wigeons often graze on land like geese, and are known to snatch water plants from diving ducks and coots as they surface.

name: Willet
hint: Large grey sandpiper that flashes bold black-and-white wing stripes in flight
fact: The willet is named after its loud, ringing call, often written as 'pill-will-willet'.

name: Wing
hint: Feathered forelimb that lets most birds fly
fact: A bird's wing is a modified arm with a shoulder, elbow and wrist. The long primary flight feathers are anchored on fused hand bones.

name: Wingspan
hint: Tip-to-tip measurement of a bird with its flight limbs fully spread
fact: A wandering albatross caught in 1965 had a wingspan of 3.63 metres (11 ft 11 in), the official record for any living bird.

name: Wishbone
hint: Forked part of a roast bird two people tug apart for luck
fact: The wishbone, or furcula, is made of fused collarbones and flexes like a spring as a bird flaps. Tyrannosaurus rex had one too.

name: Woodcock
hint: Plump, long-billed forest wader with eyes set so far back it can see all around
fact: A group of woodcocks is called a 'fall'. The flexible tip of a woodcock's long bill can open underground to grab earthworms.

name: Woodcreeper
hint: Brown Neotropical climber that props on a stiff tail as it hitches up trunks
fact: Woodcreepers of the Americas look like Old World treecreepers but are only distantly related, a classic case of convergent evolution.

name: Woodlark
hint: Short-tailed streaky songbird of heaths and clearings; pale eyebrows meet in a V at the nape
fact: The woodlark's scientific name, Lullula arborea, echoes its liquid 'lu-lu-lu' song, which it often sings in circling song flights, sometimes even at night.

name: Woodpecker
hint: Tree-drumming bird with a chisel beak and stiff tail feathers used as a prop
fact: Woodpeckers have very long tongues that wrap around the skull when retracted, and stiff tail feathers that brace them against trunks while they drum.

name: Woodswallow
hint: Soft-grey songbird of Australasia and Asia that glides after insects and huddles in rows on branches
fact: Woodswallows are among the few songbirds that soar and glide. They often huddle tightly together in rows on branches.

name: Wren
hint: Tiny brown songbird that often cocks its short tail upright; very loud for its size
fact: Despite being tiny, the Eurasian wren has a remarkably loud song. A wren was pictured on the British farthing coin from 1937 until the coin was withdrawn.

name: Wrentit
hint: Small, long-tailed songbird of California's chaparral, a lifelong homebody
fact: Wrentit pairs mate for life and may spend their entire lives within a territory of just a few acres.

name: Wrybill
hint: New Zealand plover whose beak bends to one side
fact: It is the only bird in the world whose beak bends sideways in one direction, always to the right; it uses it to reach insects under riverbed stones.

name: Wryneck
hint: Woodpecker relative that writhes its head and hisses like a snake when disturbed at the nest
fact: Wrynecks can turn their heads almost 180 degrees. Unlike true woodpeckers they don't dig their own nest holes, and they feed mainly on ants.

name: Zygodactyly
hint: Foot arrangement with two toes forward and two back
fact: Parrots, woodpeckers and cuckoos grip with this kind of foot, while owls and the osprey can swivel an outer toe to switch between arrangements.
